* feat(cloudformation, apigw-v2): support AWS::ApiGatewayV2::Authorizer

AWS::ApiGatewayV2::Authorizer had no CloudFormation provisioner at all,
so deploying a CDK/CloudFormation stack with a JWT authorizer on an
HttpApi (e.g. HttpUserPoolAuthorizer) failed outright with "Unsupported
resource type" and rolled the whole stack back -- even though the same
authorizer already worked end-to-end when created via Terraform's
aws_apigatewayv2_authorizer or the raw CreateAuthorizer API (see #802),
and is already enforced correctly at request time.

Add _apigw_v2_authorizer_create/_delete, mapping CFN properties onto the
same in-memory authorizer store the control-plane API already writes to.
jwtConfiguration is normalized from CFN's PascalCase Audience/Issuer to
the API's camelCase wire shape, matching how GetAuthorizers actually
serializes the response.

Also fix AWS::ApiGatewayV2::Route, which read AuthorizationType from CFN
properties but silently dropped AuthorizerId and AuthorizationScopes --
so even after adding the Authorizer resource, a route referencing one
would deploy but never actually invoke it at request time.

Adds test_cfn_apigwv2_authorizer_jwt: deploys an HttpApi + JWT Authorizer
+ Route referencing it, and asserts the authorizer and route come back
correctly through the control-plane API.

feat(kms): add GenerateDataKeyPair and GenerateDataKeyPairWithoutPlaintext (#1107)

The emulator implemented GenerateDataKey/GenerateDataKeyWithoutPlaintext
but had no data key *pair* operation, so both actions returned
InvalidAction: Unknown action. Add both, provisioning an asymmetric data
key pair whose private key is wrapped under a symmetric CMK:

- GenerateDataKeyPair returns PrivateKeyPlaintext, PrivateKeyCiphertextBlob
  and PublicKey; the WithoutPlaintext variant omits PrivateKeyPlaintext so
  the private key never reaches the caller in the clear.
- KeyPairSpec follows the real AWS enum (RSA_2048/3072/4096,
  ECC_NIST_P256/P384/P521, ECC_SECG_P256K1, ECC_NIST_EDWARDS25519; SM2
  excluded, as CreateKey does not implement it either).
- EncryptionContext binds the wrapped private key; the blob decrypts back
  to a PKCS#8 DER private key that pairs with the returned public key.

Extend the symmetric ciphertext layout with a per-blob random nonce
(key_id + ctx_hash + nonce + data) mixed into key derivation. Without it
the XOR keystream repeats across every blob sharing a CMK and
EncryptionContext, and because a key pair's plaintext embeds its public
modulus, the wrapped private key could be recovered from the public
outputs alone. Encrypt, GenerateDataKey and Decrypt adopt the same nonced
layout so every wrap/unwrap path stays consistent.

Update the KMS row in README and add a CHANGELOG entry.

fix(s3tables): make add-schema/add-spec/add-sort-order idempotent by id (#1212)

A resent add-schema, add-spec, or add-sort-order commit for an id that's
already registered (Spark's Iceberg client re-declares the current,
unchanged schema on every write) appended a second entry with the same
id instead of being a no-op. Iceberg's own schemasById()/specsById()/
sortOrdersById() build an id-keyed map from these lists and throw
IllegalArgumentException("Multiple entries with same key: 0=table {...}")
the moment any client (Spark, DuckDB) loads or re-commits the table,
permanently bricking it.

This is a structural invariant of Iceberg TableMetadata, not a matter of
retry semantics or AWS parity: real Iceberg's own TableMetadata.Builder
enforces the same "reuse if id already present" rule server-side. It is
a different question from whether add-snapshot should dedup by
snapshot-id, which is deliberately left out per the existing AWS-parity
discussion in PR #1204 (AWS relies on client-side OCC/retry rather than
server-side snapshot dedup for that one).

* fix(firehose): package duckdb for Alpine and wire CFN table schema for Iceberg delivery

Firehose's Iceberg destination (1.4.7) depends on duckdb at runtime, but
duckdb ships no musllinux wheels, so it was silently missing from the
Alpine-based image (ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'duckdb').
Compile it from source in the builder stage instead
(CMAKE_BUILD_PARALLEL_LEVEL=3 avoids OOM-killing the compiler on
DuckDB's unity-build translation units) and add its runtime shared
libs (libstdc++, libgcc) to the final stage. +~81MB image size,
+~12min build time.

With duckdb present, Firehose then failed with "Table ... does not
have a column with name ...": _s3tables_table_create (the CFN
provisioner for AWS::S3Tables::Table) hardcoded the Iceberg schema to
[], never reading IcebergMetadata.IcebergSchema.SchemaFieldList from
the template. Every CFN-created table ended up with zero columns
regardless of what schema was declared. Parse it like the direct
CreateTable API path already does.

Refs #1206.

* Revert Alpine duckdb build — use :full image variant instead

Per review: ministackorg/ministack:full already ships duckdb (from
manylinux wheels on a Debian/glibc base, per Dockerfile.full and
issue #411) specifically to avoid compiling it from source on musl.
Compiling it on Alpine was solving an already-solved problem, and
per DuckDB's own docs runs ~30% slower on musl anyway — so drop that
part of the change and keep only the CFN schema-wiring fix, which is
unrelated to which image variant is used.

schema fix applied: Firehose now actually delivers to the Iceberg
table — a real Parquet data file plus Iceberg metadata/snapshot

IoT — binary topic-rule payloads are no longer corrupted (#1253)

* fix(iot): evaluate the topic rule SELECT clause

The rules engine routed a publish to its actions but read nothing from
the rule's SQL beyond the FROM clause, so a projection was silently
dropped and every action received the whole message.

Parse and evaluate the SELECT clause (*, attribute paths, AS aliases,
topic()/topic(n), timestamp(), literals), naming unaliased items the way
AWS names them and omitting attributes the message does not carry. Both
the Basic Ingest and topic-filter delivery paths share the projection.

* fix(iot): keep topic-rule payloads binary-safe

Rule events were built from a UTF-8 decode with errors="replace", so a
payload that is not valid UTF-8 reached the action with every non-ASCII
byte destroyed — binary payloads could not travel the rule path at all.

Thread the published bytes into the projection and add
encode(<expr>, 'base64'), which encodes the payload as published, so a
rule selecting encode(*, 'base64') AS data delivers base64 that decodes
back to the published bytes. This is the documented way to reach a
Lambda action, which does not accept binary input. A payload that is not
valid UTF-8 and whose SELECT projects no attributes now dispatches
nothing rather than corrupted text.

fix(apigateway): rank HTTP API routes by specificity, not insertion order (#1256)

The HTTP API (API Gateway v2) router returned the first route whose
method and path matched in dict-insertion order, with no precedence
between an exact route (e.g. POST /api/v1/sql/execute) and a greedy
catch-all (ANY /{proxy+}). Real API Gateway always dispatches to the
most specific matching route regardless of creation order, so whichever
route happened to be registered first during terraform apply won,
silently misrouting a dedicated route onto the proxy catch-all (404 the
only symptom).

Score every matching route by specificity (literal segment count,
explicit method over ANY, non-greedy over greedy) and pick the best,
preserving the existing $default fallback.

DynamoDB Streams — backlogs and ESM read positions leaked, degrading a long-lived container (#1254)

* fix(dynamodb): expire stream records and release ESM poller state

Stream records accumulated for the life of the process: the per-table
list was never trimmed, DeleteTable left it behind, and deleting an event
source mapping left its stream position, Kinesis positions, and backoff
entry in place. A container cycling stacks with auto-named tables grew a
larger set for the poller to walk on every tick, so stream-to-Lambda
delivery slowed until it was restarted.

Expire records 24 hours after they are written, as AWS does, release a
table's backlog on DeleteTable, and release an ESM's poller state on
delete — from the CloudFormation delete paths as well as the API ones.
Read positions are now absolute stream positions tracked against a trim
horizon, so a consumer behind expired records resumes at the horizon.

* fix(dynamodb): make every stream read position absolute

Trimming expired records shifted the list every consumer indexes into, so
the Streams API's shard iterators (and EventBridge Pipes' positions) would
skip live records once a stream aged out: GetRecords read by absolute index
while the list moved underneath it.

Read positions are now absolute stream positions everywhere — shard
iterators, Pipes, and the Lambda ESM poller — resolved against the trim
horizon, and a position behind the horizon resumes there. Retention is
wall-clock, so the read paths expire records too and an idle stream ages
out without needing another write. Records with no creation timestamp are
never expired.

fix(cfn): honour KeySpec and update semantics on AWS::KMS::Key (#1304)

The AWS::KMS::Key provisioner hand-rolled its key record and hardcoded
KeySpec to SYMMETRIC_DEFAULT while reading KeyUsage from the template, so
a template asking for RSA_2048 SIGN_VERIFY reached CREATE_COMPLETE with a
symmetric key that DescribeKey reported as SIGN_VERIFY. The mismatch only
surfaced at the first kms:Sign, as UnsupportedOperationException. KeyPolicy,
Tags, Enabled and EnableKeyRotation were dropped on the same path.

_kms_key_create now delegates to the KMS service's own _create_key, so the
CloudFormation and API paths cannot disagree about what a key spec means.
KeyPolicy is mapped to the API's Policy string and CloudFormation's
{Key, Value} tags to the API's {TagKey, TagValue}. An unsupported spec now
fails the stack instead of silently becoming symmetric.

AWS::KMS::Key also had no update handler, so _update_resource fell back to
create and minted a fresh key whenever CloudFormation saw the resource
change — a silent key rotation once KeySpec is honoured. KeySpec, KeyUsage,
Origin and MultiRegion now fail the update as documented; the remaining
properties apply in place and keep the key material. Removing a key from a
stack schedules deletion honouring PendingWindowInDays rather than dropping
it from the store, and KeyMetadata surfaces DeletionDate while pending.

CreateKey gains RSA_3072, which the documented KeySpec enum includes and
_generate_data_key_pair already produced.

resource never becomes Ready.

* Paginate the CloudFormation Lambda list assertion

test_cfn_stack_with_s3_lambda_dynamodb called list_functions() without
pagination. ListFunctions defaults to MaxItems=50, so the assertion only
ever inspected the first page. Running the full parallel phase against a
single MiniStack server accumulates 160+ functions, pushing
intg-cfn-full-fn onto a later page and failing the assertion even though
the stack created the function correctly.

CI does not hit this because its 3-way shard split gives each shard its
own server, keeping every one under the 50-function page size.

Same class of bug as #1266, which paginated the equivalent assertions in
test_lambda.py; this call site was missed.

* feat(kms): add HMAC keys, GenerateMac and VerifyMac

CreateKey now supports the four HMAC key specs (HMAC_224/256/384/512).
An HMAC key requires KeyUsage=GENERATE_VERIFY_MAC; that usage is
rejected for every non-HMAC key spec, and EncryptionAlgorithms /
SigningAlgorithms are omitted from HMAC key metadata rather than
returned empty.

GenerateMac computes a real RFC 2104 HMAC using the stdlib hmac module.
VerifyMac returns MacValid: true on success, failing with
KMSInvalidMacException on any mismatch. Both operations validate the
MacAlgorithm enum, reject an algorithm that does not match the key's
spec, enforce the documented 1-4096 byte message limit (checked before
base64 decode too), bound the Mac blob before decoding it, accept key
IDs / key ARNs / aliases, respect Disabled and PendingDeletion state,
and implement DryRun. The MAC comparison runs ahead of the DryRun
check, so an invalid MAC is reported as KMSInvalidMacException:
DryRunOperationException is documented to mean the request would
otherwise have succeeded, which is not the case here.

_is_hmac_key keys off the key spec and the presence of HMAC material,
never off KeyUsage alone, so a symmetric key persisted by an earlier
build that carries GENERATE_VERIFY_MAC is not misread as an HMAC key.

Complementary key handling: HMAC keys are rejected with
InvalidKeyUsageException by Encrypt, Decrypt, Sign, Verify and
GenerateDataKey*, and with UnsupportedOperationException by
EnableKeyRotation, the only rotation operation AWS documents as
unsupported for HMAC keys. DisableKeyRotation and GetKeyRotationStatus
accept them and report rotation off, matching real AWS. Encrypt reports
InvalidKeyUsageException ahead of DisabledException, which is the order
real AWS validates in.

HMAC key material round-trips through persisted state, and
CloudFormation AWS::KMS::Key honours an HMAC KeySpec, failing the
resource when KeySpec and KeyUsage disagree. The CloudFormation test
covering an unimplemented spec moves from HMAC_256 to SM2, which this
emulator still does not support.

Error codes and validation order were taken from the AWS KMS API
reference and checked against a live account.

* fix(eventbridge): a connection's OAuth token dies with the connection

The access-token cache added with API-destination dispatch is keyed by
(account, region, connection name), and connection names are reusable,
but nothing ever evicted an entry: the token outlived the connection
that minted it. A connection deleted and recreated under the same name
— how Terraform replaces one in place — inherited its predecessor's
token and kept authorizing deliveries with credentials that no longer
applied, until the cached token happened to expire. Rotating a client
secret through UpdateConnection had the same blind spot.

The cache is now evicted when the connection is deleted, when it is
re-authorized (AuthParameters or AuthorizationType supplied to
UpdateConnection), and when it is deauthorized. A description-only
update does not re-authorize, so it keeps the cached token and makes no
needless exchange.

Three tests cover the three transitions: recreation under a reused name
re-exchanges with the new credentials, a rotated client secret takes
effect on the next invocation rather than at token expiry, and a
metadata-only update reuses the cached token.

feat(dsql): Aurora DSQL emulator with control plane and SQL-validating PG proxy (#1320)

* feat(dsql): Aurora DSQL emulator with control plane and SQL-validating PG proxy

* fix(dsql): validate the extended wire protocol and fix transaction fidelity

The DSQL proxy only validated the simple 'Q' protocol. Everything else was
relayed verbatim, so any client using prepared statements — pgjdbc, pgx,
asyncpg, psycopg3 and the ORMs on top of them — bypassed the DSQL subset
entirely: serial columns, foreign keys, CREATE EXTENSION, temp tables,
materialized views and partitioned tables were all created for real. The
gap was worst where it mattered most, since the rules that only apply to DML
(3,000-row/10 MiB limits, FOR UPDATE, DDL+DML mixing) are exactly the ones
parameterized traffic hits. The test suite could not catch any of it: it
drives the proxy with psycopg2, which interpolates client-side and always
sends 'Q'.

- Validate Parse/Bind/Describe/Execute/Close/Sync. Rejections honour
  skip-until-Sync; sys.jobs, sys.wait_for_job and the ASYNC DDL rewrites are
  synthesized on this path too, so DSQL-only syntax no longer comes back as a
  bare Postgres syntax error.
- Take transaction state from the backend's ReadyForQuery status byte instead
  of inferring it from statement text. A BEGIN or COMMIT sent over the
  extended protocol used to strand in_txn, which made the validator reject
  valid autocommit DDL with 25006 — a false rejection, worse than a missed
  one — and left the status byte lying about the block.
- Abort the transaction when the proxy rejects a statement: the backend never
  saw the error, so later statements kept succeeding and COMMIT committed
  work the client had been told failed. Now 25P02 until the block ends, and
  COMMIT of a failed block reports ROLLBACK, as Postgres does.
- Make statement splitting, comment stripping and paren matching lexer-aware.
  A ';' or ')' inside a string literal truncated the text a rule saw and the
  rule passed on the fragment; a leading -- or /* */ comment disabled the
  validator wholesale, which migration tools trip constantly.
- Classify past leading comments, CTEs and EXPLAIN ANALYZE, so CTE-leading
  writes stop escaping every DML rule.
- Deny CREATE RULE, VACUUM, CLUSTER, REINDEX, ALTER SYSTEM, prepared
  transactions, publications/subscriptions, foreign data wrappers and
  CREATE DOMAIN/CAST/OPERATOR/AGGREGATE/COLLATION.

Adds a raw wire-protocol test client, since psycopg2 cannot reach the
extended path, plus regression coverage for each of the above.

* feat(dsql): refuse to drop a primary key column

Aurora DSQL added ALTER TABLE ... DROP COLUMN on 2026-08-03, with several
columns allowed in one statement but not primary key columns. DROP COLUMN
already passed validation, so only the new restriction was missing.

Knowing which columns form the primary key needs a catalog probe, so the
check lives in the statement planner next to the FOR UPDATE key check rather
than in validate(): it applies to both wire protocols and is skipped in
pipelined extended-protocol batches, like the other probe-backed rules. The
pg_index lookup FOR UPDATE already ran is now shared.

The COLUMN keyword is optional in Postgres, so DROP CONSTRAINT / DEFAULT /
NOT NULL / EXPRESSION / IDENTITY have to be told apart from a bare column
name; quoted identifiers that collide with those keywords still count as
columns.

* dsql: make backend containers opt-in (DSQL_CONTAINERS) with configurable cap

Default is now control-plane-only stubs: CreateCluster returns ACTIVE
metadata-only clusters. DSQL_CONTAINERS=1 restores real per-cluster
Postgres containers behind the wire proxy, capped by DSQL_MAX_CONTAINERS
(default 30); exceeding the cap logs a warning and degrades the cluster
to a stub.

* dsql: e2e container test + review fixes for opt-in backends

- Add TestContainersE2E: in-process end-to-end test (Docker-gated) that
  flips DSQL_CONTAINERS on, creates a cluster, and runs SELECT 1 through
  the wire proxy against the real Postgres container.
- CI: start MiniStack with DSQL_CONTAINERS=1 so the existing live
  data-plane test keeps exercising real backends.
- Fix cap-slot leaks: clear _has_backend on respawn failure and for
  restored stubs; restored stub clusters no longer resurrect containers.
- Rename MAX_CLUSTERS -> MAX_CONTAINERS to match DSQL_MAX_CONTAINERS.
- Note that the container cap is deliberately not re-enforced on restore.

fix(cloudformation): resolve AWS::SSM::Parameter::Value<...> against SSM (#1338)

* fix(cloudformation): resolve AWS::SSM::Parameter::Value<...> against SSM

A template parameter typed AWS::SSM::Parameter::Value<String> (or
<List<String>> / <AWS::EC2::Image::Id>) takes an SSM parameter name as
its value; real CloudFormation resolves that name against Parameter
Store before Ref ever sees it. MiniStack passed the literal name
through unchanged, so Ref returned the parameter's name instead of its
stored value. Resolution now looks the name up via the SSM store; a
name that doesn't exist fails CreateStack/UpdateStack synchronously
with a ValidationError, matching AWS.

* fix(cloudformation): don't re-resolve an already-resolved SSM parameter value

UsePreviousValue reuses a prior deployment's already-resolved Value for
an AWS::SSM::Parameter::Value<...> parameter (see the resolved dict this
loop builds) — that value is a final value, not an SSM parameter name to
look up again. The fresh SSM-lookup added by the previous commit ran on
it anyway, so updating a stack that reuses such a parameter (e.g. CDK
re-sending its own BootstrapVersion, unrelated to this fix, on every
deploy) failed because the already-resolved value almost never happens
to also be a valid SSM parameter name.

* fix(cloudformation): EventBus survives a stack update

AWS::Events::EventBus has no update handler, so _update_resource falls
back to calling create again on every stack update (documented as
relying on create being idempotent, same as SQS/SNS). Its create wasn't:
it unconditionally rejected an existing name with "already exists". A
name baked into the template client-side (e.g. CDK's EventBus construct,
which computes its default name from the construct path) is identical
on every deploy, so any stack containing one failed every single update,
even when the bus itself hadn't changed.

Discovered while end-to-end testing the AWS::SSM::Parameter::Value<...>
fix against a real multi-stack deploy that updates a stack containing
one of these buses.

fix(cloudformation): resources unchanged by a stack update are left alone (#1340)

* fix(cloudformation): resources unchanged by a stack update are left alone

_update_resource was reprocessing every previously-provisioned resource
on every stack update, even when nothing about it changed, then (for any
type with no dedicated update handler) falling through to calling create
again. Two bugs compounded there: the fallback passed physical_id where
create expects logical_id, and _physical_name generated a fresh random
suffix on every call — so an auto-named resource's "idempotent" create
silently produced a brand new, empty resource under a new identity on
every single update, orphaning the real one. Anything referencing it via
Ref/Fn::GetAtt (itself reprocessed later in the same update, since real
CloudFormation does propagate a changed reference) picked up that new,
wrong identity the moment it was resolved.

_update_resource now short-circuits when a resource's properties are
genuinely unchanged, matching real CloudFormation, which doesn't touch
such a resource at all. _physical_name's suffix is now a deterministic
hash of (stack_name, logical_id) rather than random, and the no-handler
fallback passes the real logical id — both matter for the remaining case
where a resource's properties did change but the type still has no
update handler, so its "idempotent" create needs to reproduce the same
name it started with.

Found via a DynamoDB table silently duplicating on an unrelated update
to a real multi-stack deploy; also fixes the same symptom for any other
resource type with no update handler and no self-idempotency guard of
its own (e.g. AWS::Events::EventBus, which previously failed a stack
update outright with "already exists" once created).

* docs: changelog entry for the resource-update-idempotency fix

fix(ec2): revoke security group rules by SecurityGroupRuleId (#1346)

RevokeSecurityGroupIngress and RevokeSecurityGroupEgress ignored
SecurityGroupRuleId.N parameters and returned Return=true without
removing anything, so a rule addressed by id — how Terraform's
aws_vpc_security_group_ingress_rule destroys one — survived every
revoke and stayed in DescribeSecurityGroups and
DescribeSecurityGroupRules.

Both handlers now resolve the ids against the group's stored
content-derived sgr-* rule ids, remove the matched rules and their rule
tags, and echo the revoked rules in revokedSecurityGroupRuleSet (both
directions, as the botocore model declares it on the ingress result
too). An unknown id rejects the whole call with
InvalidSecurityGroupRuleId.NotFound before anything mutates, matching
AWS.

Two things a reviewer will want to know up front:

- The by-id path returns revokedSecurityGroupRuleSet, while the
  pre-existing IpPermissions path on ingress still returns a bare
  <return>true</return>. That path is deliberately untouched, so no
  existing response shape changes here.
- If one request carries both SecurityGroupRuleIds and IpPermissions,
  the ids win and the permissions are ignored, whereas AWS rejects the
  combination. A documented divergence rather than a silent one; the
  rejection can be added if upstream prefers it.

only a property mismatch yields the 409. Mirror the pattern
_create_thing already uses — normalize so absent, None and empty
properties compare equal on both sides, return the stored
thingTypeName/thingTypeArn/thingTypeId on a match, keep the 409 for

fix(lambda): report docker/RIE handler failures as Unhandled (#1348)

The Docker/RIE executor marked every error payload as Handled whenever
the RIE response carried no X-Amz-Function-Error /
Lambda-Runtime-Function-Error-Type header, so a failed invocation
surfaced as X-Amz-Function-Error: Handled and API Gateway consumers
depending on the 502-for-Unhandled contract never took the error path.

Probing the RIE bundled with public.ecr.aws/lambda/python:3.12,
nodejs:22 and provided:al2023 shows that no error header is returned on
the invocation response — not for a raised handler exception, and not
even when a custom runtime POSTs its own
Lambda-Runtime-Function-Error-Type to /runtime/invocation/<id>/error
(the RIE drops it and logs RTDONE(status: success) either way). So
classification has to key on the payload shape, and that shape differs
per runtime: python sends stackTrace — empty for init failures such as
Runtime.ImportModuleError — nodejs sends trace, and go / provided.*
send no traceback field at all. An error-shaped payload ({errorType,
...}) therefore reports Unhandled unless it also carries a statusCode,
which marks an HTTP-style envelope the handler returned itself
(Handled). Testing one stackTrace key for truthiness would have left
import errors and every nodejs and go failure on the Handled path.

A handler that *returns* a bare {errorType, errorMessage} dict is
indistinguishable from a go-style runtime error over this wire and is
reported Unhandled on the docker executor; that is the safe direction,
since only Handled-instead-of-Unhandled breaks the 502 contract. The
local (default) executor is unaffected — it classifies from the raise
itself and still sets no FunctionError for a returned dict.

The decision is extracted into a pure
_classify_function_error(parsed, err_header) helper called by
_invoke_rie, unit-tested in-process over the four observed runtime
payload shapes plus the header-present, statusCode and non-error cases.

feat(stepfunctions): support aws-sdk:route53 tasks (#1361)

* fix(stepfunctions): name rest-xml SDK errors after the exception class

_dispatch_aws_sdk_rest_xml returned the wire <Code>, so a failing S3 op came back
S3.NoSuchBucket where real Step Functions reports S3.NoSuchBucketException. Measured on five
ops against a bucket that does not exist, so a Catch written against AWS does not fire here.

The same pass makes the dispatcher service-agnostic: the op-spec table, the error prefix and
the path placeholders belong to the protocol but were S3's. Requests are unchanged.

* feat(stepfunctions): support aws-sdk:route53 tasks

route53 was not in _AWS_SDK_SERVICE_MAP, so every aws-sdk:route53:* Task failed at dispatch
while the identical boto3 call against the same server worked. Adds the service and a
ChangeResourceRecordSets spec, the one operation with a caller behind it.

Two things are Route 53's own and both are silent when wrong: it wraps XML lists
(<Changes><Change/></Changes>) where S3 repeats the parent element, and it nests Code/Message
under <Error> with a default xmlns, so find("Code") misses. The hosted zone id is substituted
verbatim -- fix_route53_ids is a boto3 handler Step Functions does not run, and AWS rejects
the prefixed form. Path and body are asserted byte-identical to botocore's serialiser.

* fix(stepfunctions): send rest-xml body members under their wire names

_dispatch_aws_sdk_rest_xml passed body member names through verbatim where the json and
query dispatchers convert them. Step Functions only accepts the SDK spelling at
CreateStateMachine ("Did you mean 'Ttl'?"), and route53 does not read <Ttl>, so the record
was stored with no TTL while the execution still succeeded. Of the thirty member names
across the S3 and route53 specs it changes exactly one.

fix(apigatewayv2): invoke and enforce REQUEST (Lambda) authorizers (#1362)

HTTP API (v2) routes support two authorizer types: JWT and REQUEST
(Lambda). _handle_execute_in_scope only ever branched on
`auth_type == "JWT"`, so a route with `AuthorizationType: CUSTOM` (the
type a route gets when it references a REQUEST authorizer -- the
authorizer resource's own `authorizerType` is REQUEST, but the route's
AuthorizationType enum has no REQUEST value, confirmed against the
apigatewayv2 CreateRoute/CreateAuthorizer service models) fell through
exactly like an unauthenticated `NONE` route. The authorizer Lambda was
never invoked -- not for a missing token, an invalid one, or a valid
one -- and requestContext.authorizer was always undefined downstream.

This is the same gap 1.4.16 closed for REST (v1) TOKEN/REQUEST
authorizers (apigateway_v1._authorize_request_v1), left open for HTTP
API (v2): the fix that shipped in 1.4.16 was scoped to REST only (see
ministackorg/ministack#1345, item 1).

Adds a REQUEST-authorizer data-plane path (_authorize_request_v2)
mirroring the v1 fix's shape, adapted to HTTP API's own conventions:

- Honors `authorizerPayloadFormatVersion`: 1.0 builds a REST-shaped
  event (methodArn, multiValueHeaders, etc.) and only accepts an IAM
  policy response; 2.0 builds the newer event shape (routeArn,
  rawPath/rawQueryString, identitySource, http.*) and accepts either
  the simple `{isAuthorized, context}` response when
  `enableSimpleResponses` is set, or the same IAM policy response
  format as 1.0 otherwise.
- Evaluates IAM policy responses against the route ARN the same way
  v1 evaluates them against a method ARN (explicit Deny always wins,
  Allow requires a matching statement and no Deny).
- Honors `authorizerResultTtlInSeconds` caching, including the
  missing-identity-source short-circuit v1 uses (a declared identity
  source that's absent is a 401 without invoking the Lambda, only
  when caching is on).
- Populates `requestContext.authorizer.lambda` for the downstream
  AWS_PROXY integration event (JWT authorizers deliver under `.jwt`
  instead), and wires the same context into
  `$context.authorizer.lambda.*` for HTTP_PROXY request-parameter
  mappings, mirroring the existing JWT-claims mapping support.

Adds two data-plane tests covering both 2.0 response formats (simple
and IAM policy), verified to fail against the pre-fix code (a denied
token silently passed through with 200) and to pass with the fix
applied; also verified by hand against a from-source Docker build that
the authorizer Lambda is now actually invoked (confirmed via its
CloudWatch Logs stream) for missing, invalid, and valid tokens, with
requestContext.authorizer.lambda populated on the integration side.

Addresses (in part) ministackorg/ministack#1345 (item 1's HTTP API v2
gap; the fix that landed in 1.4.16 covered REST/v1 only, and the other
7 unrelated items from that report are out of scope here).

fix(eventbridge): validate and contain the API destination outbound request (#1365)

An API destination target makes an outbound HTTP request that carries the
connection's credentials to a URL the caller chooses. Every value on that
path was taken on trust. Six fixes, all on that one path:

- Do not follow redirects on delivery or OAuth token requests. urllib
  keeps the Authorization header across a cross-host 3xx, leaking the
  connection credentials to the redirect target; a 3xx is now a
  non-retryable delivery failure, as on AWS.
- Reject an InvocationEndpoint at Create/UpdateApiDestination, and an
  OAuth AuthorizationEndpoint at Create/UpdateConnection, that is not a
  dialable http(s) URL; the outbound opener independently refuses
  non-HTTP(S) schemes, so file:// and friends never reach the wire even
  for a record restored from persisted state. The scheme is compared
  case-insensitively, as URL schemes are. A non-empty authority is not
  sufficient: "http://@" and "http://:80" carry no host, and urlsplit
  strips CR/LF/TAB before it reports one, so "http://ho\nst/x" would be
  dialed as a host the caller never wrote.

  This is a scheme guard, not a network guard. MiniStack is a local
  emulator where delivering to 127.0.0.1 is the normal case, so
  loopback, private and link-local hosts stay reachable over http(s) by
  design.
- Validate HttpMethod and a connection's AuthorizationType against their
  API enums. Both were stored verbatim: an unrecognized method silently
  became POST on the request line, and an unrecognized authorization
  type matched nothing in the auth-header builder, so the connection
  delivered with no credentials at all.
- Re-apply the removed-header filter and fixed headers after merging the
  connection auth headers, so an ApiKeyName of User-Agent/Host cannot
  override EventBridge's reserved headers. Names are matched trimmed:
  "User-Agent " is not in the removed set, and http.client only rejects
  whitespace as the first character of a name, so the padded spelling
  rode out beside the real one.
- Make DeauthorizeConnection do what the API reference says it does —
  "removes all authorization parameters from the connection" — and skip
  delivery for a connection that is not AUTHORIZED. It flipped the state
  and evicted the cached OAuth token but left the credentials in place,
  so every later delivery still presented them; the OAuth eviction
  achieved nothing, because the next delivery fetched a fresh token.
- Read the OAuth token response with a 1 MiB bound, the same ceiling
  EventBridge's fixed Range header puts on a delivery response, rather
  than unbounded from a caller-supplied endpoint.

AuthParameters is type-checked rather than dereferenced, so a non-object
value keeps its existing behaviour instead of becoming a 500. The urllib
imports are hoisted to module level, replacing the per-call local
imports the delivery helpers used, and the README's EventBridge row
records the behaviour that changed.

SECURITY.md keeps unintended host compromise in scope even for a no-auth
local tool. Sixteen regression tests added, four of them in-process: the
opener-level scheme guard, the header filter, the OAuth token path and a
non-object AuthParameters are all unreachable from the boto3 harness.

feat(lambda): layer-version permissions — API trio + the CFN resource (#1371)

Deploying a Serverless Framework stack whose serverless-python-requirements
layer sets `allowedAccounts` (or a CDK stack calling
`LayerVersion.addPermission`) failed on MiniStack: the generated
`AWS::Lambda::LayerVersionPermission` resource had no provisioner, so the
whole stack died with `Unsupported resource type` and landed in
ROLLBACK_COMPLETE.

Adds the CloudFormation resource type, mapped onto the existing
AddLayerVersionPermission / RemoveLayerVersionPermission service calls. The
type has no StatementId property — the statement id is generated by the
resource provider and surfaces only through the resource's `Id`, which is the
layer version ARN and the statement id joined by `#`. Deriving that id from
(stack name, logical id) via `_physical_name` keeps it stable across updates:
every property of this type is create-only, so a property change is a
replacement, and with no update handler the framework re-runs create (#1340) —
which now lands on the same statement instead of failing the update with
ResourceConflictException. Delete revokes the grant and tolerates a layer
version that a rollback already removed.

The three layer-permission APIs were routed but a few details did not match
the Lambda model:

- `RevisionId` was a fresh UUID minted per call, so it could not be used for
  anything. The policy now carries a revision id, bumped on every successful
  mutation and reported by GetLayerVersionPolicy; passing a stale one to
  Add/RemoveLayerVersionPermission fails with `PreconditionFailedException`
  (412) rather than clobbering a policy that changed underneath the caller.
- `Principal` was not validated and was written into the policy document
  verbatim. It is now checked against the model's pattern (12-digit account,
  `*`, or a root user ARN), and an account id renders as
  `{"AWS": "arn:aws:iam::<account>:root"}` the way the policy document reports
  it on AWS. An `OrganizationId` alongside a non-`*` principal is rejected
  with `InvalidParameterValueException`, matching the CDK-side check.

Scope: as everywhere else in MiniStack, the grants are recorded but not
enforced — GetLayerVersion does not consult the policy, since there is no IAM
enforcement anywhere in the emulator. The store is the existing
account/region-scoped layer state, so it rides along with get_state /
restore_state / reset and survives a persistence round-trip.

fix(tls): minted leaf certificates carry an Authority Key Identifier (#1369)

sign_leaf_certificate built every leaf with basicConstraints, keyUsage,
extendedKeyUsage and subjectAltName, but no Authority Key Identifier.
RFC 5280 §4.2.1.1 requires one on any certificate that is not
self-issued, so the omission is not merely cosmetic: Python 3.13 turns
on ssl.VERIFY_X509_STRICT inside ssl.create_default_context(), and a
strict verifier rejects such a leaf outright with

  certificate verify failed: Missing Authority Key Identifier

That is the default client configuration, so on a current Python nothing
MiniStack minted could be verified against the CA that signed it.
CreateKeysAndCertificate hands those certificates to devices, and the
IoT mTLS listener mints its broker certificate through the same helper,
so the failure reaches both ends of a connection. The self-signed CA
from generate_ca() is exempt by the same rule and is left alone; it
already carries the matching SubjectKeyIdentifier, which is what the new
extension points at.

tests/test_x509_utils.py is new. Rather than assert on an extension list
alone, it verifies a minted leaf the way a client does — a real TLS
handshake between the two ends of a socketpair, the client built by
ssl.create_default_context() with its strict flag left on, so the test
fails for the same reason and with the same message a user would see.
Two narrower cases sit beside it: the identifier must match the issuing
CA's SubjectKeyIdentifier rather than merely exist, and the CA itself
must stay self-signed and free of one.

Validation:
- tests/test_x509_utils.py: 3 passed with this change; reverting only
  the extension turns it into 2 failed / 1 passed, the handshake failing
  on "Missing Authority Key Identifier" and the self-signed-CA case
  correctly unaffected — the test was confirmed to fail without the fix,
  not just to pass with it
- tests/test_tls.py: 5 passed (the gateway's USE_SSL certificate is
  self-signed through the openssl CLI in core/tls.py and is untouched)
- tests/test_iot.py: 87 passed, the whole file, covering
  CreateKeysAndCertificate and the certificate registry
- ruff clean on both touched files

fix(apigatewayv2): scope the REQUEST-authorizer cache to the route ARN (#1370)

The REQUEST-authorizer path added in #1362 caches the allow/deny *verdict*
under `(api_id, authorizer_id, "|".join(identity_values))`. AWS caches the
authorizer's *response*: "By default, API Gateway uses the cached authorizer
response for all routes of an API that use the authorizer" — the response is
what carries over, so the canonical `Resource: event['routeArn']` policy
that every AWS sample emits is still evaluated per request and still grants
only the one route it was issued for. Caching the verdict instead lets one
Allow answer every other guarded route the same identity touches, on every
stage, in every account (`_authorizers` is an AccountRegionScopedDict).

The cache now stores the authorizer's OUTPUT — the policy document and the
context — keyed per (account, region, api, authorizer, stage, identity
values), and re-evaluates the policy against each request's own route ARN.
A hit still avoids the Lambda invocation; it just cannot grant what the
policy does not. A simple response has no resource dimension ("the
authorizer's response fully allows or denies all API requests that match the
cached identity source values"), so there the verdict itself remains what is
cached — only the key is widened.

Four smaller faults in the same path:

- A simple response was accepted on truthiness, so a returned
  `{"isAuthorized": "false"}` — a truthy string — authorized the request.
  `isAuthorized` must now be a real boolean; anything else is an invalid
  response format, which the docs map to a 500, matching this path's own
  error handling.
- A response without a `policyDocument` evaluated as an implicit deny (403)
  and was cached under that verdict. It is the same invalid-format 500, and
  an invalid response is now the only thing never cached: a returned Deny
  still caches for the full TTL, as AWS does.
- `int(authorizerResultTtlInSeconds or 0)` raised on a non-numeric value —
  UpdateAuthorizer copies the request body verbatim and never validates it —
  and conflated an absent TTL with an explicit 0. Both now fall back to the
  documented default `_DEFAULT_AUTHORIZER_TTL`, which CreateAuthorizer uses.
- The cache never evicted, and with no identity source declared it keyed
  every caller under the empty list, serving the first caller's result to
  everyone at the default 300s TTL. Caching now requires an identity source
  ("To enable caching, your authorizer must have at least one identity
  source"), and writes drop expired entries and cap the cache.

This follows the REST (v1) fix — 1.4.16's data plane plus our follow-up in
`apigateway_v1._authorize_request_v1` — and the same shapes were flagged
here while #1362 was still in review.

feat(iot): fleet indexing — SearchIndex over the live registry, behind the index switch (#1382)

Fleet code that calls SearchIndex could not be exercised against the
emulator at all: the operation was unimplemented, so every query failed
at the router.

SearchIndex (POST /indices/search) now evaluates AND-separated
field:value terms over thingName, thingTypeName, thingGroupNames,
attributes.<name> and shadow.desired|reported.<path> directly against the
live registry and shadow stores — there is no projection to build, so
results are always current. Values compare case-insensitively and accept
* (any run) and ? (one character), because a prefix query such as
thingName:my-fleet-* is what a fleet dashboard actually sends; other
characters match literally, so a bracket in a thing name is not read as an
fnmatch character class. A JSON number in a shadow compares numerically, so
a reported {"temp": 10.0} answers shadow.reported.temp:10 the way a typed
index does, while registry strings keep comparing as strings — a thing named
007 is not a hit for thingName:7. A hit carries thingName, thingId,
thingTypeName, thingGroupNames, attributes and the classic shadow as a JSON
string document, as on AWS; because both halves of the state are queryable,
the document carries desired as well as reported. Results page through
maxResults + nextToken (an offset cursor, ceiling 100) instead of the two
being documented and then ignored.

The index has to be enabled first, which is a behavior change for anyone
already calling SearchIndex against this emulator.
UpdateIndexingConfiguration / GetIndexingConfiguration / DescribeIndex /
ListIndices are implemented, thingIndexingMode defaults to OFF exactly as on
a fresh AWS account, and searching while it is OFF answers
ResourceNotFoundException ("Index 'AWS_Things' does not exist") rather than
quietly working. Enabling it is what Terraform's aws_iot_indexing_configuration
does first, and requiring it here is what stops fleet code from passing
locally and then failing against an account nobody turned indexing on for.
REGISTRY_AND_SHADOW is what makes shadow.* queryable; under REGISTRY the
shadow terms are rejected and hits carry no shadow document. DescribeIndex
reports ACTIVE and never BUILDING — the registry is the index, so it is ready
the moment it is switched on. AWS's model lists both IndexNotReadyException
and ResourceNotFoundException on SearchIndex; DescribeIndex carries only the
latter, so "does not exist" is the shape for indexing being off and
IndexNotReadyException belongs to a BUILDING index this emulator never has.
The connectivity, Device Defender and named-shadow modes are stored and
echoed back so IaC round-trips, but nothing projects those fields yet;
querying one is an out-of-grammar error, not a silent miss.

The query parser walks tokens rather than deleting the terms and inspecting
the remainder, so a malformed query is an error instead of a silent no-op: a
bare word that is not AND, a leading or doubled AND, and a dangling AND with
no right-hand term all answer InvalidQueryException (400), which is what real
AWS does with them. Unknown fields answer the same way — shadow spellings
outside desired/reported included, since a typo and a field no thing carries
are indistinguishable in an empty result set and only one of them is the
caller's bug.

Not modeled: OR / NOT, ranges, connectivity.* and the other fleet-index
metadata fields, named shadows, thing-group aggregation queries, and
searching thing-group documents — all rejected as out-of-grammar rather than
silently returning nothing.

Validation: tests/test_iot.py + tests/test_persistence.py, 345 passed
against a live server, up from 333. Nine new tests cover the indexing-config
round trip (default OFF, enable, DescribeIndex / ListIndices, back to OFF),
the rejected impossible modes, searching before enabling, shadow terms under
REGISTRY-only indexing, thing-group membership terms, maxResults / nextToken
paging to exhaustion, rejected paging arguments, unknown shadow subfields,
and numeric shadow comparison. The five existing SearchIndex tests enable
indexing in setup, which is what real usage looks like. ruff clean on the
touched files.

test_cfn_unnamed_dynamodb_table_survives_unrelated_update compared the

* feat(sesv2): add email template CRUD and Content.Template rendering

CreateEmailTemplate, GetEmailTemplate, UpdateEmailTemplate, DeleteEmailTemplate and ListEmailTemplates are served at /v2/email/templates[/{TemplateName}] over the shared v1 template store, so a template created through either API version is visible to the other.

SendEmail now renders Content.Template resolved from TemplateName, from a template ARN, or from TemplateContent supplied inline; a named template that does not exist fails the send with NotFoundException (404) instead of delivering an email with an empty subject and body.

fix(iot): unsubscribe only the topic filters the packet names (#1379)

The MQTT-over-WebSocket bridge's UNSUBSCRIBE branch read the packet id and
then dropped every subscription the session held, without ever parsing the
topic-filter list that follows it. A client that unsubscribed from one topic
went silent on all of them. The sids were cleared while _sub_filters was left
untouched, so a cleanSession=0 disconnect also preserved the filter the client
had just unsubscribed from, and a resume resurrected it.

Parse the payload and remove only the subscriptions whose filter matches one
of the names, compared character-by-character as MQTT 3.1.1 3.10.4 requires:
a wildcard subscription goes by its own filter string, never by a topic it
happened to match, and a filter that matches nothing is skipped. The
comparison reads _sub_filters, which holds the filter as it arrived on the
wire — the multi-tenancy prefix is applied inside broker_subscribe, so
comparing against the prefixed form would have matched nothing at all. The
three per-session maps are now cleared together, which is what makes the
preserved-session case symmetric. A truncated payload unsubscribes the filters
that did parse and logs, rather than tearing the session down.

MQTT 3.1.1's UNSUBACK carries no reason codes, so the acknowledgement is
unchanged whether or not a subscription existed. The v5 UNSUBACK reason codes
on our MQTT 5 branch already report per-filter truth (0x00 success,
0x11 no subscription existed); they only become accurate once this lands.

Part of #1343.

Validation: tests/test_iot.py + tests/test_iot_data.py, 117 passed against a
live server, 111 before. Six new tests, and all five in-process ones fail on
the previous behaviour: only the named filter is removed while the others keep
delivering; an unknown filter is a no-op that still gets its UNSUBACK; naming
every filter stops delivery and empties the session maps; a wildcard filter
survives an unsubscribe of a topic it matched and goes on its own text; an
unsubscribed filter stays out of a preserved cleanSession=0 session. The sixth
drives the one-of-two-filters case over the real WebSocket bridge and fails
against an unpatched server. ruff check clean on the three touched files.

fix(lambda): map host.docker.internal to host-gateway in containers (#1375)

On a native Linux Docker engine, the first thing a docker-executed handler did
when it called back into MiniStack was die on DNS: "<urlopen error [Errno 16]
Device or resource busy>", on the very first invocation, before any request

fix(apigateway): scope v1 authorizer cache to method ARN and stage (#1367)

A CUSTOM method's Lambda authorizer returns the canonical
`Resource: event['methodArn']` policy — an Allow for exactly the one method
it was issued for. 1.4.16 cached the resulting allow/deny *decision* under
`(api_id, authorizer_id, token)`. That key carries no method ARN and no
stage, so within `authorizerResultTtlInSeconds` a single Allow answered
every other guarded method the same bearer token touched, and answered it
on every stage of the API. The policy's own `Resource` scope was evaluated
once and then never consulted again.

The cache now stores the authorizer's OUTPUT — its policy document and
context — keyed per (account, region, api, authorizer, stage, identity
values), and the policy is re-evaluated against each request's own method
ARN. A cache hit still avoids the Lambda invocation; it just cannot grant
what the policy does not.

Four smaller faults in the same path:

- `re.fullmatch(identityValidationExpression, token)` was unguarded.
  CreateAuthorizer stores the expression verbatim, so an uncompilable one
  raised `re.error` out of the handler and the client received the parser's
  message ("unterminated character set at position 6") as the response body.
  It is now a 500 AUTHORIZER_CONFIGURATION_ERROR.
- `int(authorizerResultTtlInSeconds)` was unguarded, and absent vs.
  unparsable disagreed (0 vs. an exception). UpdateAuthorizer applies JSON
  Patch without validating, so the field can be any string by the time the
  data plane reads it. Both cases now fall back to the same documented
  default, `_DEFAULT_AUTHORIZER_TTL`, which CreateAuthorizer also uses.
- A response without `principalId` was allowed through with an empty
  principal reaching the backend, and one without a `policyDocument` was
  evaluated as an implicit deny (403) and cached; AWS treats both as the
  500 configuration error and never caches it.
- The cache never evicted. Its keys include caller-supplied bearer tokens,
  so a long-lived instance grew one entry per distinct token ever seen.
  Writes now drop expired entries and cap the cache.

fix(iot): topic-rule WHERE evaluation, SQL functions, non-Lambda actions (#1380)

* fix(iot): evaluate topic-rule WHERE clauses and validate rule SQL

Topic rules dispatched on the FROM topic filter alone: the WHERE predicate
was never consulted, so WHERE-carrying rules over-fired on every matching
publish. The engine now parses the predicate and gates dispatch on it,
reusing the SELECT expression evaluator for scalar resolution. The grammar
covers what real AWS rules are written in — comparisons (=, ==, <>, != plus
<, >, <=, >=), IN / NOT IN, LIKE / NOT LIKE, BETWEEN, IS [NOT] NULL, a bare
boolean attribute, isUndefined(), and regexp_matches(), composed with AND, OR
and NOT under AWS's precedence (OR loosest, then AND, then NOT) and regrouped
by parentheses, which may abut a keyword rather than being separated by
whitespace, as in "(a = 1)AND(b = 2)". Operands are attribute paths, numbers,
function calls, string literals (where a doubled '' is an escaped quote), and
arithmetic over those: + - * / %, the multiplicative three binding tighter.

Evaluation is three-valued, as AWS's is. Every operator answers Undefined for
an operand it cannot use, Undefined composes as SQL says (it loses to a true
OR sibling and a false AND sibling, survives the rest), and only a predicate
that comes out true fires the rule. Two-valued evaluation would agree
everywhere except under NOT, where it is exactly wrong: NOT of a clause over
an absent attribute would fire, where AWS leaves it Undefined. So it fails
closed however it is reached.

The one place operand types are settled is AWS's published conversion table,
which each operator coerces through rather than deciding for itself — the
alternative being the drift where regexp_matches(temp, '^2') matched
{"temp": 22} because it went through str() while temp LIKE '2%' did not,
because it demanded a Python string. Both now convert, as does an ordering
comparison over a numeric string; equality still does not convert, so a
mismatched pair is simply unequal.

SQL the parser cannot evaluate is rejected up front, and that check now sits
inside put_topic_rule (raising RuleSqlError) rather than at three call sites,
so both doors into the store are covered: the HTTP handlers translate it to
SqlParseException, and RuleSqlError is a ValueError, which is already what
fails an AWS::IoT::TopicRule resource. Only malformed SQL is rejected —
anything real AWS accepts has to create here too, or a stack that deploys on
AWS fails locally. Rules calling a function this evaluator does not implement
are likewise stored rather than rejected, since AWS's function library is
larger than ours, but such a call resolves to Undefined, so put_topic_rule
warns at creation and the expression evaluator warns on first use; a stored
predicate that cannot be parsed at all (state written by an older MiniStack)
also warns instead of looking like a quiet non-match. That scan discounts
SQL's own keywords: matching <name>( alone read the brackets in "WHERE (",
"IN (" and "AND (" as calls and warned about a missing where()/in()/and().
The warn-once ledger the warning keeps is module state, so reset() clears it.

The three quote/paren scanners the splitters need are one shared
_top_level_indices helper, which the arithmetic splitter reuses and which also
anchors the malformed-input rejection (unterminated literal, unbalanced
parentheses) in a single place.

* feat(iot): add newuuid, replace and clientid to rule SQL

The rule SQL expression evaluator knew only topic(), timestamp() and
encode(); every other function resolved to the missing-value sentinel, so
its field silently vanished from the projection and a WHERE clause over it
never matched. newuuid() mints a fresh UUID per evaluation,
replace(expr, 'from', 'to') rewrites string values (a missing or non-string
source stays Undefined, as on AWS, and both literals take the SQL doubled-''
quote escape), and clientid() reports the publishing MQTT client's id,
threaded as a new broker_publish keyword from the WebSocket PUBLISH handler
through _evaluate_topic_rules and _run_rule_actions into the projection
context — and, like any operand, through every WHERE leaf form and the
arithmetic operands those can sit inside. The HTTP publish path passes no
client id, so there clientid() resolves to the sentinel and the field is
omitted, matching real AWS for HTTP publishes.

principal() and traceid() stay accepted at rule creation, because a rule
using them deploys on AWS, but this publish path carries no certificate
identity or trace id to report: they resolve to the sentinel and warn, like
any other function the evaluator does not implement.

Typed feat rather than fix: these are AWS rule SQL functions MiniStack did
not support, not a regression in ones it did.

* feat(iot): dispatch republish, dynamoDBv2 and sns topic-rule actions

Only lambda actions ever executed; republish, dynamoDBv2 and sns were stored

no boto3). republish feeds the projected event back through broker_publish at
the action's qos, with a depth-8 contextvar guard so a rule republishing onto
its own matching topic (user error — AWS does not loop-protect either) is cut
and logged instead of recursing forever. dynamoDBv2 maps each projected
attribute to a DynamoDB AttributeValue column and calls dynamodb._put_item.
sns goes through a new sns.publish_internal, which is the body _publish itself
now wraps, so a rule-published message gets the same normalization, 256 KiB

already were — and each action dispatch is guarded individually: a failure

fix(apigateway): non-proxy lambda integrations return raw output (#1376)

A REST method wired to a non-proxy AWS (custom, "lambda") integration
answered nothing like real API Gateway. A handler returning a plain dict
such as {"statusCode": 418, "body": "x"} came back as HTTP 418 with the
body "x" instead of HTTP 200 carrying that whole dict; a handler whose
output had no statusCode key came back as an empty 200. A raised
exception surfaced the function's error payload (errorMessage,
errorType) to the caller.

_handle_execute_in_scope routed int_type in ("AWS_PROXY", "AWS") into
_invoke_lambda_proxy_v1, which is written for the proxy contract: it
reads the return value as a {statusCode, headers, body} envelope and
promotes those keys onto the HTTP response. A non-proxy integration has
no envelope — the function's return value IS the response body, handed
back with the integration response's status code.

The two types now split. AWS_PROXY is untouched; AWS goes through a new
_invoke_lambda_custom_v1 that JSON-serializes the raw return value as
the body (Content-Type application/json) with the status of the
integration response whose selectionPattern is empty, 200 when none is
configured. A function error answers 502 {"message": "Internal server
error"}, as on AWS, so the error payload never reaches the caller.

Both types are invoked with the same event, so the payload format 1.0
build is extracted into _build_lambda_event_v1 and shared; they differ in
how the response is read, not in what the function is called with.
Likewise the invoke itself now exists once: _call_lambda_raw performs it
and returns the execution record, and _call_lambda is that plus the
AWS_PROXY response shaper. The two were otherwise line-for-line
identical, which is a bad way to keep the scoped-lookup and
central-dispatcher behaviour in sync between the two integration types.
requestTemplates and responseTemplates mapping templates remain
unmodeled, as documented on the new helpers.

fix(lambda): report RIE init failures and timeouts, don't retry them (#1374)

A Lambda whose handler module cannot be imported never came back. RIE answers
such an invocation with HTTP 502 and the init-error payload, and urllib raises
that as HTTPError — a subclass of URLError, so it landed in _invoke_rie's
connection-refused arm, which sleeps 100ms and re-POSTs. Every retry makes RIE
run INIT again (it resets the sandbox after a failed init), so the loop
hammered the container for Timeout * 10 + 20 attempts: fifteen minutes at ten
failed inits a second for the 900s timeout a serverless deploy sets. Invoke
blocked for all of it, and under any concurrency the storm took the emulator
down with it — on PERSIST_STATE=0 the restart then wipes every service's state.

A handler that blows its Timeout took the same wrong turn. The read timeout on
an already-accepted POST is a socket.timeout, which is an OSError, so it also
fell into the cold-start arm and re-POSTed the event — running the handler
again, from the top, for the whole attempt budget — then reported the raw
"Lambda RIE failed: <container logs>". Measured on a Timeout=3 function: 7.9s
and the wrong error shape.

The distinction the loop could not make is between "nothing is listening yet",
a cold start still coming up, and "the runtime answered", which no retry will
change. _rie_failure_is_retryable makes it explicit: an HTTPError is an answer;
a bare TimeoutError means the request was accepted and the handler ran past its
timeout; everything else — refused connections, resets, a URLError wrapping a
connect timeout — stays retryable, so a genuine cold start still gets its
retries (verified: 6.8s cold starts on a Timeout=3 function, 6/6 ok).

A terminal failure is shaped the way AWS shapes it, HTTP 200 with
X-Amz-Function-Error: Unhandled and the error payload in the body, which the
existing function-error plumbing already carries to the caller. A timeout
reports "Task timed out after N.00 seconds" / Runtime.ExitError — the message
and type the local executor and this file's own docker catch-all already emit,
so all three executors agree on one shape.

A timed-out container is also recycled instead of pooled. Its handler is still
running inside the RIE, so handing it to the next invocation would queue that
one behind a zombie; AWS terminates the execution environment on a timeout and
this is the same bargain, at the cost of a cold start. The teardown runs off
the response path (SIGTERM grace + SIGKILL takes seconds) so the caller still
sees the error at the timeout mark.

Belt and braces, the reconnect phase now has a wall-clock deadline of
min(Timeout + 2s, 30s). The old attempt budget was derived from Timeout alone,
so a container that never listens at all could still hold its caller for the
full fifteen minutes. RIE binds its port in about a second, so 30s is a
generous ceiling, and the deadline is never longer than the previous budget.

The 502 is not an assumption: three POSTs to an unimportable handler on
public.ecr.aws/lambda/python:3.12 each return 502 with
{"errorType": "Runtime.ImportModuleError", ...}, one "INIT REPORT" and one
"Reset initiated: ReleaseFail" per request.

The timeout half of this change was previously carried by
fix/lambda-reentrant-invoke, which fixed the same _invoke_rie except clause
incompatibly. It lives here, with the rest of the classification it belongs to;
that branch keeps the worker-pool fix and no longer touches this path.

feat(lambda): enforce RecursiveLoop with a per-request depth counter (#1378)

A Lambda that invokes itself asynchronously never stopped. Each hop returns
202 and releases the warm worker immediately, so no resource is ever
exhausted and nothing bounds the chain: a probe function ran 25 hops in
under 20 seconds and only stopped because the handler had a hardcoded stop
condition of its own.

PutFunctionRecursionConfig stored RecursiveLoop and GetFunctionRecursionConfig
read it back, but no invoke path ever consulted either, and nothing counted
how many times a request had already been around a function. The API was
present and inert.

Invocations now carry a lineage counter, the way AWS does it -- counting hops
on the request rather than concurrent executions, which is what catches a loop
whose every hop finishes before the next one starts. `_invoke` reads the
inbound depth, adds one, and drops the request with the AWS-modelled
RecursiveInvocationException (HTTP 400) plus a RecursiveInvocationsDropped
metric once it passes 16, unless the function's RecursiveLoop is Allow.

16 is the number of invocations that run, not the first one refused: the
Developer Guide says Lambda "automatically stops the next function invocation"
once a function is invoked "approximately 16 times in the same chain of
requests". So hop 17 is the first one dropped. AWS hedges with
"approximately"; ministack counts exactly, and the tests pin that.

How the counter travels
-----------------------

The depth reaches a child through its environment -- through the event for the
warm workers, whose env is fixed at spawn time. Both worker bootstraps move it
into the environment and drop the key, so a handler never sees it in its
payload.

It comes back on the nested call as a request header,
X-Ministack-Invoke-Depth:

- Python children: the bootstrap appends a before-call handler to botocore's
  BUILTIN_HANDLERS, alongside botocore's own add_recursion_detection_header.
  It runs after sys.path is assembled, so a function that bundles its own
  botocore gets that one, and before the handler module is imported, because
  botocore copies BUILTIN_HANDLERS into every Session it builds and handlers
  routinely build their clients at import time. The price is importing
  botocore on every cold start: a trivial function's first invoke goes from
  0.11s to 0.27s here.
- Node children: the worker's bundled Lambda client stamps the same header
  from process.env. A Node function that brings the real
  @aws-sdk/client-lambda in a layer is not instrumented.

AWS carries this counter on the X-Ray trace header. Ministack does not: two
existing tests pin the shape of the _X_AMZN_TRACE_ID that ministack hands to
functions, and widening it to carry a lineage field would change what every
traced function reads. A separate header keeps the two concerns apart, at the
cost of not being wire-compatible with AWS's version of the same idea.

That header is client-forgeable. Deliberately so: there is no trust boundary
between a local caller and the local gateway, and being able to set the depth
by hand is what lets a test reach the limit in one hop instead of sixteen.

What this catches: direct Lambda -> Lambda hops, sync and async, from Python
or Node handlers on the warm workers, and from Python on the one-shot
subprocess executor.

What it does not catch, and why:

- Loops that leave through another service and come back (Lambda -> SQS / SNS
  / S3 / EventBridge -> Lambda). The counter rides on the Invoke request only,
  so the return leg starts a fresh lineage. AWS threads the same counter
  through the event payload; this does not.
- Hops through API Gateway, ALB, or a Function URL. Depth is established in
  `_invoke`, so a gateway-mediated call restarts at 1.
- Outbound calls from a docker RIE container. `_spawn_lambda_container` now
  bakes the depth into the container env, but its containers are pooled and
  reused, so the value is the one from the invocation that cold-started the
  container -- the same staleness that already applies to the durable-execution
  overlay next to it -- and ministack owns no bootstrap inside the container to
  stamp it onto outgoing calls. Inbound drops still apply to docker functions,
  because that check lives in `_invoke`.
- Warm-worker invocations whose payload is not a JSON object, which have
  nowhere to carry the depth.

A *synchronous* self-invoke never ran away in the first place, for an
unrelated reason: the warm worker holds a per-function lock, so the nested
call blocks until the caller times out. That is untouched here, except that
the guard now fires before the lock is taken, so a sync self-invoke past the
limit fails fast instead of wedging.

Cost on the normal path is one dict lookup and an integer compare per invoke.

CloudWatch Logs until the chain settles; the other three assert on wall clock.

Node one, which is a single hop.

fix(app): combine repeated request header lines instead of keeping the last (#1388)

The ASGI header dict was built with plain assignment, so a field a client
sent twice kept only its final line. The AWS SDK for Java v2 uploads
exactly that way -- Content-Encoding: gzip and Content-Encoding:
aws-chunked on separate lines -- so MiniStack saw only aws-chunked,
stripped it as the chunk-framing marker it is, and stored the object with
no content encoding at all, silently losing the caller's gzip.

Repeated field lines now combine into one comma-joined value as RFC 9110
5.2 requires, with Cookie rejoining on "; " per RFC 9113 8.2.3. Stripping
aws-chunked from the joined list leaves the caller's encoding behind, as
it already did for a client that sent the header once.

fix(s3): answer the conditional-read headers on GetObject and HeadObject (#1390)

If-Match, If-None-Match, If-Modified-Since and If-Unmodified-Since were
honoured on PutObject, CopyObject and DeleteObject but ignored on the
reads, so every conditional read returned 200 and the whole body. A cache
revalidating an unchanged object refetched it in full, and a read guarded
against a concurrent overwrite never noticed one.

Reads now answer 412 PreconditionFailed or 304 Not Modified with the
precedence RFC 9110 13.2.2 and the AWS GetObject reference define: an
entity tag decides, and its date counterpart applies only in its absence.
The check runs before the Range and partNumber slicing, so a failed
precondition preempts the read instead of slicing a representation the
caller already rejected.

The 304 keeps the validators the 200 would have carried and drops the
headers describing a payload it cannot send. x-amz-checksum-* is among
them: boto3 requests checksum validation by default, and one on a body-less
response makes it wrap the empty body in a validating stream it then fails
to parse -- the same hazard that already keeps checksums off a 206.

feat(iot): device shadows over MQTT (#1395)

The HTTP shadow APIs worked, but publishing to the reserved shadow topics
did nothing — device SDKs update shadows exclusively over MQTT, so no real
device client could sync state locally. A publish (WS MQTT or HTTP Publish;
both funnel through broker_publish) to
$aws/things/<thing>/shadow/get|update|delete — classic or
/name/<shadowName>/ named form — now feeds the same in-process shadow core
as the HTTP data plane, pinned under request_scope because the WS path sets
only the account contextvar, and publishes the AWS reserved-topic responses
back through the broker at qos 1: accepted with the response document
(clientToken echoed when the request carried one), rejected with
{code, message} (400 malformed, 404 missing, 409 version conflict), plus
update/delta (state + metadata + version + timestamp, only when
desired != reported, and carrying the triggering request's clientToken as on
AWS) and update/documents (previous/current documents + timestamp).

Both documents are stripped of their delta section before publishing.
get_thing_shadow injects state.delta (and metadata.delta) by design, because
that is what a GET answers with, and the documents topic is not a GET: on AWS
a documents state carries desired and reported only, and the delta has its own
topic — published just above, from the same update. Passing the snapshot
through verbatim invented a section no real device ever receives.

previous is deep-copied at capture: get_thing_shadow returns the stored
state dicts themselves and update_thing_shadow merges into them in place, so
an un-snapshotted previous reports the state after the update and, from the
second update on, is the same document as current. current is snapshotted
for the same reason.

An empty named shadow (.../shadow/name//update) names nothing; rather than
silently collapsing onto the classic shadow — writing the wrong record and
answering on a topic the requester is not subscribed to — it is rejected on
the named form's own reply topic.

The bridge hooks in AFTER subscriber delivery and rule evaluation, so rules
on $aws/things/+/shadow/update fire on the request, and the recursive
accepted publish drives datasync-style rules on
$aws/things/+/shadow/update/accepted; response suffixes parse as
non-requests, so the bridge never re-triggers itself. Its call is guarded
like the other two side effects in broker_publish: it was the only unguarded
one, so anything it raised that the inner handler does not catch (a deeply
nested document raises RecursionError out of json.loads) tore down the
caller's MQTT session.

Known divergence (pre-existing, unchanged): _topic_matches lets a bare
`#` subscription match `$aws/...` topics, unlike real AWS, where `#`
excludes the reserved topic space.

Malformed JSON rejects with a 400 on the requester's own `rejected`
topic for all three request verbs, as on AWS — a `get`/`delete` payload
is optional but must parse when present, instead of being silently read
as `{}`.

feat(iot): dispatch the sqs topic-rule action (#1396)

CreateTopicRule stores actions verbatim, so a rule carrying an sqs action
was accepted and handed back by GetTopicRule unchanged — and then did
nothing when its topic fired. Only lambda was ever dispatched, so the most
common non-Lambda fan-out in real fleets could not be rehearsed locally even
though the emulator has a full SQS service sitting right next to it.

The rule's evaluated payload is now delivered to the queue named by
queueUrl. useBase64 base64-encodes the message body, which is what the field
means on AWS: the consumer receives Base64 text and has to decode it, it is
not a transport hint. roleArn is accepted and ignored, as everywhere else in
the emulator — there is no IAM evaluation to fail.

Delivery goes through the SQS service's own code rather than an HTTP
SendMessage, the way the SNS and EventBridge fan-outs already do, so a rule
firing while the gateway is busy cannot deadlock on itself. It reuses
sqs._get_q and sqs._act_send_message rather than reimplementing them —
stepfunctions' sqs:sendMessage task is the precedent — and that reuse is
what makes the enqueued message an ordinary one: the queue's DelaySeconds
and MaximumMessageSize apply, the body character check applies, and the
MessageId is the dashed UUID every other producer mints, not a shape no real
SQS message has. The rules engine runs on the broker's task with no ambient
request scope, so the call is wrapped in request_scope for the account and
region the publish was made in, as the dynamoDBv2 and sns actions are; and
_get_q's own URL-then-name resolution is what lets a rule written against
localhost still reach a queue created through a different host alias.

A failed delivery raises, like every other dispatcher behind
_dispatch_rule_action. Per-action isolation is the collector's job in
_run_rule_actions — the rule's remaining actions still run — and the failure
now also reaches the rule's errorAction instead of dying in a log line.
SQS's wire error is translated to a plain exception at the boundary, again
as stepfunctions does, so the failure document reads as a sentence. A
queueUrl naming another account is refused by _get_q rather than silently
resolved to a same-account queue of the same name, since the cross-account
grant AWS would require has no local equivalent.

FIFO destinations are refused with a warning before the send. AWS documents
them as unsupported for this action — the rules engine is distributed, so it
cannot promise the ordering a FIFO queue exists to provide — and enqueuing
anyway would need a MessageGroupId we would have to invent.

Builds on the _dispatch_rule_action table that landed with the topic-rule
WHERE/actions change: dispatchers raise and their failures feed the rule's
errorAction; sqs is one more entry in it.
Bolted onto the old loop with a swallow of its own, as this branch first
did, sqs would have been the one action whose failures never reached
errorAction.

Part of #1343 (§2.3, which names dynamoDBv2, sns and republish; sqs is the
same gap).

feat(iot): CA-certificate registry and registration events (#1397)

GetRegistrationCode / DeleteRegistrationCode (GET|DELETE /registrationcode)
mint a stable per-account/region sha256-hex code, persisted; delete discards
it and the next get mints a fresh one.

RegisterCACertificate (POST /cacertificate) takes caCertificate (+ optional
verificationCertificate) in the body and setAsActive / allowAutoRegistration
as query params, per the botocore model. The CA id is derived like device
certificate ids (SHA-256 of the DER) with ARN form
arn:aws:iot:{region}:{account}:cacert/{id}; a duplicate CA PEM answers the
shared ResourceAlreadyExistsException 409 carrying resourceId/resourceArn.
DescribeCACertificate returns the PEM verbatim with status and
autoRegistrationStatus. UpdateCACertificate applies newStatus /
newAutoRegistrationStatus from the query string per the model, falling back to
the JSON body the way UpdateCertificate already does — a body-only request
used to be a 200 that applied nothing. ListCACertificates lists the registry,
and DeleteCACertificate refuses an ACTIVE CA with CertificateStateException
(406, per the service model).

RegisterCertificate validates caCertificatePem before it stores anything: the
named CA has to be registered in this account and region, and it has to be the
certificate that really signed the leaf — issuer/subject DN as the cheap
discriminator, then the signature itself against the CA's public key, in the
new x509_utils.certificate_is_signed_by. Either miss is a
CertificateValidationException, 400 per the service model. Taking the caller's
word for it meant a leaf signed by CA-X could register as CA-Y's: the JITR
event then fires on CA-Y's topic, and a JITR Lambda that picks its provisioning
template by caCertificateId provisions the wrong fleet.

When that CA is ACTIVE and has auto-registration enabled — an INACTIVE CA
auto-registers nothing on AWS — the lifecycle event {certificateId,
caCertificateId, timestamp, certificateStatus, awsAccountId,
certificateRegistrationTimestamp} is published to
$aws/events/certificates/registered/{caCertificateId} through the in-process
broker, where a topic rule picks it up and hands it to its Lambda, and
DescribeCertificate resolves the signing CA. That publish is wrapped and logged
at WARNING: the certificate is already committed by then, so a broker failure
must not turn a successful registration into a 500 — the iot-data publish path
guards the same call the same way.

Registration stays explicit. There is no first-connect mTLS trigger, so
nothing auto-registers a certificate the way a real device's first handshake
does, and registrationConfig is accepted and ignored, so provisioning
templates do not run.

Companion fix: the pre-existing device-certificate DELETE answered
CertificateStateException with 409 while the new CA delete answers 406, the
status the service model gives that exception. Both are 406 now.

Both new stores (_ca_certificates, _registration_codes) are account/region
scoped and wired through get_state/restore_state/reset.

Test hygiene alongside. The topic-rule test binds its rule to its own CA id
rather than the + wildcard: the registered-certificate topics are shared per
account, so a wildcard rule live for the length of that test also catches the
registrations other xdist workers make, and _poll_sink returns whichever event
lands first — cross-talk reproduced deterministically on the wildcard form and
gone on the exact topic. test_iot_registration_code_stable_until_deleted joins
_SERIAL_TESTS: DeleteRegistrationCode is an account-global mutation, the same
class as the IAM entries already listed there. And the persistence test now
asserts both stores are gone after reset() as well as present after
restore_state() — an after-restore assertion alone passes even when nothing was
restored, as long as reset() left the value standing.
