fix(eventbridge): match event patterns the way AWS does (#1404)

Event-pattern matching diverged from real AWS in ways that were verified
against it, and the quieter failures were the worse ones: several
patterns made a rule match every event and fan it out to its targets,
others made a rule that looks right locally filter out everything in
production, and a pattern AWS refuses outright was accepted here.

Semantics throughout come from aws/event-ruler, the engine EventBridge
runs, because the user guide is silent on most of what decides them.

Patterns are validated. PutRule, TestEventPattern, CreateArchive and
UpdateArchive checked only that a pattern was valid JSON; everything past
that was accepted. That is the expensive direction for an emulator,
because the operands AWS refuses are largely the ones this emulator could
not evaluate: the local answer was silence where production gives a 400.
All four now reject with InvalidEventPatternException carrying AWS's own
reason text. numeric turns out to be a grammar rather than a list of
pairs, so [">", 1, ">", 2] and ["=", 1, "<", 5] are refused. A malformed
$or falls back to being read as an ordinary field name, as EventBridge
does. Every fail-closed guard stays in the matcher behind that door: a
rule restored from persisted state is loaded verbatim and never
revalidated.

- Wildcard matching used fnmatch, which treats ? and [seq] as special and
  handles the \ escape backwards. Only * is special now, \ escapes, and
  ? and [seq] are literal. A correctly-escaped guard pattern matched
  locally but never matches on AWS, so a rule that works against
  MiniStack silently filters out everything in production. The translator
  keeps the property fnmatch had for free: each interior literal is
  emitted as (?=(?P<gN>.*?lit))(?P=gN), so it cannot backtrack
  catastrophically on the dispatch path.
- A malformed operand reached a Python builtin and raised, surfacing as
  HTTP 500 instead of AWS's 400 — from TestEventPattern and from
  dispatch, where it aborted the enclosing PutEvents rather than failing
  one rule. A numeric operand with an unrecognized operator, or truncated
  to fewer than a full pair, fell out of the comparison loop and returned
  true, so the rule matched every event.
- anything-but inverts its nested matcher, so an operand the matcher
  could only answer "no match" to inverted into that same
  match-everything rule. It only inverts what AWS lets it nest —
  prefix, suffix, wildcard, equals-ignore-case, singly or as a list —
  and the gate scans every key the matcher dispatches on, since
  approving on one key while the matcher answers on another is how the
  inversion reopens.
- cidr, equals-ignore-case, exactly and case-insensitive prefix/suffix
  were accepted and then fell off the end of the dispatch, answering "no
  match" for every event. cidr compares addresses rather than text,
  floors host bits, reads octets as decimal, and refuses /32 and /128 as
  AWS does; only a string can match it, since ipaddress reads an integer
  as an address. equals-ignore-case accepts either case of each operand
  character on its own, which is neither lower() nor casefold(): the
  first cannot match straße against STRASSE, the second also accepts
  strasse. The relation is asymmetric and not reflexive for a titlecase
  character, as on AWS.
- A top-level $or was not read at all, and an unread key is a matched
  key, so a pattern whose only key was $or matched every event on the
  bus. It is expanded at rule creation into one alternative per branch,
  which is how AWS's per-leaf last-write-wins collision rule falls out:
  {"a":["1"],"$or":[{"a":["2"]},{"b":["3"]}]} matches a="2" and not
  a="1", and writing the two keys the other way round reverses both.
  A recursive evaluator answers order-independently and gets both wrong.
  AWS's 1000-combination cap is enforced, counted over the $or arrays the
  pattern text holds rather than over what a compiler made of them — so a
  $or that turns out not to be the operator still counts toward it. Event
  Ruler has no cap at all, the check living only in closed EventBridge
  code, so where the text count and the fallback reading disagree the
  pattern is refused: a rule that passes locally and is refused at PutRule
  is the more expensive answer.
- The walk evaluated six envelope keys and skipped the rest, so a pattern
  filtering on id, time or version matched every event. AWS has no
  envelope allow-list — it compiles a pattern to paths — so the matcher
  is now one generic walk over the delivered envelope: an unrecognized
  key is a path the event lacks, and {"nonesuch": [{"exists": false}]}
  matches everything for that reason. resources is an intersection, not
  a requirement, and content filters work on it. replay-name is stamped
  onto replayed events, which is what AWS's own archive rule needs. Both
  the matched view and the delivered payload come from one builder, since
  two hand-kept copies of one envelope drift, and a rule matching on a
  field whose delivered value differs is invisible until production. That
  also gives delivery the matcher's reading of Detail: a Detail that is
  not JSON matched a rule and then raised out of delivery, surfacing as a
  500 that took every other rule on the bus with it, where it is now
  delivered as the string leaf it is. InputTransformer held a third copy,
  and it disagreed: <aws.events.event.json> rendered time as the raw epoch
  second the entry carried while the plain target beside it received the
  ISO-8601 string, and rendered a non-JSON Detail as {} — a field the
  event does not have. Both substitutions are the event itself now, which
  is what AWS puts there. One tree per event also means the payload is
  decoded once for the event rather than once per target.
- An array value was matched by literal intersection, so no content
  filter reached its elements; AWS flattens it, and for a pattern object
  under an array of objects one element must satisfy the whole of it,
  which is AWS's array-consistency rule. exists asks whether the path
  reaches a leaf, so an object, an empty array and an empty object do
  not exist while a null does. Equality is JSON equality: a string never
  equals a number and true never equals 1.
- Six ways a pattern or an event could take the handler down, each found
  by differential fuzzing rather than by review: a cidr mask of more than
  the 4300 digits Python will convert; an integer literal of that length
  anywhere in a pattern, which raises a plain ValueError out of the
  parse; a lone surrogate before a wildcard fault, whose byte offset
  cannot be encoded; a $or nested past the stack, which the JSON parse
  gives out on first; an event array nested past it too; and a time no
  platform clock can represent, which raised while building the view
  every pattern is matched against. A RecursionError there does not stay
  inside its own request, since handlers run on a pooled worker thread.
- Two quadratic paths on the dispatch path: the IPv6 admission regex
  (53s on a long colon-only operand) and the case-insensitive suffix.
  The compiled pattern is cached and the event view is built once per
  event with its detail decoded only if a rule reads it, so a bus of
  envelope-only rules no longer parses a payload nothing looks at — and a
  rule that names detail but fails on source does not reach it either,
  which on a shared bus is otherwise every event paying for the first
  rule that happens to filter on detail. Those memos are dropped by the
  state-reset endpoint along with the rules that wanted them: each is
  keyed on what a caller sent, nothing else evicts an entry below the
  cap, and a cache of near-cap $or expansions retains a few hundred
  times the pattern text that produced it.

Documented in the CHANGELOG rather than fixed here: the 4096-character
pattern limit, AWS's wildcard-complexity refusal, its 256-leaf rule-size
cap, and six corners — a dotted pattern key, a duplicated JSON key
hiding a fault, a fractional literal that does not survive conversion to
a double, an IPv4-mapped IPv6 mask width, exists:false beneath an array
of objects, and a leaf/object path collision across a $or boundary.

Sixty-five regression tests added, including wildcard and case-folding
rows verified against real AWS behaviour, the operands AWS refuses with
the reason it gives for each, AWS's documented $or example and its
collision cases in both key orders, dispatch-path cases, bounds on every
path that was quadratic, a case exercising every operand anything-but may
invert in both the single and the list form, and a guard that every
operator the validator accepts has a matcher to answer it — the gate's
key set is derived from the matcher's own registry, so the two cannot
drift apart, and an operator accepted at rule creation that nothing can
answer is the failure this whole change set exists to fix.

feat(iot): MQTT 5.0 support negotiated per connection (#1398)

The CONNECT parser stepped over the protocol level byte without reading
it ("off += 1  # Protocol Level"), so every connection was decoded and
answered as MQTT 3.1.1. An MQTT 5 CONNECT carries a property length field
3.1.1 does not, so the client id came off the wrong offset and the client
got a 4-byte 3.1.1 CONNACK back. Measured against the AWS IoT Device SDK
v2 (C++), that kills the client inside its own decoder with
AWS_ERROR_MQTT5_DECODE_PROTOCOL_ERROR (5149) and nothing server-side
explains why — anything built on Aws::Iot::Mqtt5ClientBuilder could not
talk to the emulator at all.

The protocol level now selects the wire format for the whole connection
and is stored on the session, so a 3.1.1 publisher and a 5.0 subscriber
interoperate through the one registry, each framed for its own version.
An unsupported level is refused with a 3.1.1 CONNACK carrying return code
0x01: that is the one shape whose second body byte every MQTT decoder
reads as a return code, which turns a silent decode failure into a
diagnosable rejection.

MQTT 5 adds property blocks on CONNECT (will properties included),
CONNACK, PUBLISH, PUBACK, SUBSCRIBE, SUBACK, UNSUBSCRIBE, UNSUBACK and
DISCONNECT; the subscription options byte, which replaces 3.1.1's bare
QoS byte; v5 reason codes; an assigned client identifier when the client
sends an empty one; Clean Start and Session Expiry Interval driving
resumption and retention separately, where 3.1.1 derives both from one
flag; and pass-through of the PUBLISH properties a server has to forward
(payload format, content type, response topic, correlation data, user
properties), which is what a request/response client needs to see its own
correlation data come back. Properties the broker does not model are
parsed and dropped, never echoed back — the parser knows the width of
every defined identifier so it can step over what it ignores.

All four fields of the options byte are acted on, not just the QoS bits.
No Local drops a delivery whose publishing client is the subscriber
itself, which is why broker_publish now takes the publishing client id —
an HTTP Publish or a rule has no client identity and so is delivered to
everyone. Retain As Published forwards the publisher's RETAIN flag
instead of clearing it, resolved per subscriber because two subscribers
to one message can legitimately see different flags. Retain Handling
picks whether a SUBSCRIBE replays retained messages always, only when the
subscription is new to that client, or never.

A property block's declared length now bounds every value read out of it.
It did not before: a block declaring one byte and holding only an
identifier had its value read from the byte *after* the block, so a
PUBLISH's payload silently donated its first byte to a property the
publisher never sent and the subscriber received both the phantom
property and a truncated payload, with nothing raised anywhere. The same
block at the very end of a packet raised IndexError instead, which
handle_websocket's broad except swallowed into a dead connection — no
CONNACK, no DISCONNECT, nothing for the client to read. Values are now
parsed out of a slice that ends where the block ends, so the existing
readers' truncation checks become the block's own bounds, and the answer
is the protocol's: MQTT 5 §4.13.1 says a server that detects a Malformed
Packet closes the connection and says why first, so a v5 session gets
reason code 0x81 — in a CONNACK when the CONNECT itself is what failed
and none has gone out yet, in a DISCONNECT once the connection is up.
3.1.1 has neither a CONNACK return code for this nor a server-sent
DISCONNECT, so there the connection just closes, per §4.8. The catch sits
at the single dispatch point rather than in the WebSocket loop, so a
transport reusing the session inherits the behaviour.

Session Expiry Interval is stored and honoured as an interval rather than
read as a boolean: 0 means do not persist, 0xFFFFFFFF means never expire,
and anything else is how long the stored session outlives its connection,
in place of the module-wide default that used to apply to every session
whatever it asked for. Timed expiry is not implemented — nothing reaps
sessions on a schedule. Expiry is evaluated when a session is looked at,
on reconnect and when a QoS 1 message hunts for offline sessions to queue
for, so an expired session is never resumed and never queued for, but its
entry survives until something touches that key. A connection that
resumes a session without persisting one — Clean Start 0 with no Session
Expiry Interval, which MQTT 5 allows because it splits the two — now
deletes the stored session on close. Nothing used to: the entry outlived
every such connection, queueing QoS 1 messages nobody would collect and
answering the next CONNECT with session_present=1. A stored session keeps
its topic filters but not the options they arrived with, so a resumed
subscription comes back at the defaults; that and the missing reaper are
documented in the module, since the protocol has no flag to advertise
either.

Deliberately out of scope, and advertised as unavailable in CONNACK
wherever the protocol has a flag for it: shared subscriptions, topic
aliases, message expiry, flow control (receive maximum) and subscription
identifiers.

MQTT 3.1.1 keeps its wire format, with one deliberate exception. Every
new field is written only when the negotiated version is 5, and the codec
lives entirely in _WSSession and the packet builders, so a transport that
reuses them (a raw TCP listener feeding the same session) inherits 5.0
without changes. The exception is one bit: a retained message replayed
because a subscription was just established now carries RETAIN 1, for
3.1.1 subscribers too. §3.3.1.3 requires it in both versions and the
broker sent 0, which leaves a client unable to tell stored state from
live traffic on the same topic — and with Retain As Published implemented
above it, leaving that bit wrong would have made the option meaningless.

This builds on the UNSUBSCRIBE fix that is now on main. That change
is what makes UNSUBSCRIBE remove only the topic filters the packet
names instead of every subscription the session holds, and the 5.0
UNSUBACK reason codes here are read off that per-filter removal: Success
(0x00) where a filter was actually removed, No subscription existed (0x11)
where the client held none. Derived any other way — from a snapshot of the
session's filters taken before an unsubscribe-everything loop — the reason
codes come out identical while the session silently loses subscriptions
the packet never named, so the two changes only make sense together.

Part of #1343.

fix(cognito): build federation endpoints from the user pool domain (#1407)

CreateUserPoolDomain accepted CustomDomainConfig and discarded it, always
expanding Domain to {Domain}.auth.{region}.amazoncognito.com, while the SAML
ACS URL and the OIDC federation callback ignored the pool's domain entirely
and were built from MINISTACK_HOST/GATEWAY_PORT. Federated sign-in therefore
handed external identity providers
redirect_uri=http://localhost:4566/oauth2/idpresponse — unreachable from the
browser, and rejected outright by Google and other public IdPs for the scheme
alone — so the flow died at the hop to the IdP with no way to correct it.

CustomDomainConfig now distinguishes a custom domain (a full FQDN, served
as-is, reported as CustomDomain on DescribeUserPool and fronted by a
CloudFront distribution) from a prefix domain (a bare label, still expanded
to the regional host). /saml2/idpresponse and /oauth2/idpresponse are derived
from whichever the pool has — including the AssertionConsumerServiceURL in
the generated SAML AuthnRequest and the redirect_uri replayed on the
back-channel token exchange, which must match — exactly as AWS derives them.

Configuring one is the same create-user-pool-domain --custom-domain-config
CertificateArn=... call you would make against AWS; no new env var. The
certificate is recorded, not served: TLS for a custom domain is terminated by
whatever fronts it (nginx, an ALB, CloudFront) and proxied to the gateway.

A pool holds one domain of each kind independently, a CustomDomainConfig
without a CertificateArn is an InvalidParameterException, and a pool with no
domain still falls back to the local gateway, so existing setups are
unchanged.

feat(iot): connectivity.* terms in the fleet index (#1399)

A fleet dashboard's first question is "which of my things are online right
now", and SearchIndex had no way to answer it: the connectivity.* group AWS
exposes once thing indexing is configured with THING_CONNECTIVITY_INDEXING
was neither queryable nor present in the returned document, so that flow
could not be rehearsed against the emulator at all.

The broker already knew the answer. It keeps a session registry per
(account, region, client id) — that is how duplicate-client eviction works —
but nothing outside the broker could read it, and nothing recorded when a
session started or why it ended.

connectivity.connected, connectivity.timestamp (epoch ms of the last
transition) and connectivity.disconnectReason now join the query grammar,
and every hit carries the connectivity group — once
thingConnectivityIndexingMode is STATUS, which is the switch AWS puts it
behind and which the fleet-indexing configuration on main implements. With it OFF the group is absent and a connectivity term is an
InvalidQueryException, so a fleet dashboard that forgets to ask for
connectivity indexing finds out here rather than in the cloud. The group is
closed either way, so an unknown leaf such as connectivity.online is
rejected rather than quietly matching nothing.

A thing counts as connected while a session whose client id equals the thing
name is live. That is the association AWS makes and the only one available
here: a device connecting under a different client id is legitimately not
that thing's connectivity, even if it is the same hardware. connected is
read from the session registry on every query rather than stored, so the two
cannot drift apart.

Only the three disconnect reasons the broker can actually tell apart are
reported: CLIENT_INITIATED_DISCONNECT (a DISCONNECT packet),
DUPLICATE_CLIENTID (a takeover) and CONNECTION_LOST (the transport went
away). AWS's remaining reasons name machinery this broker does not have —
throttling, credential expiry, keep-alive enforcement — so reporting one
would be a guess dressed up as a fact.

DUPLICATE_CLIENTID is reported on the winning session's record rather than
being written and immediately overwritten. The eviction and the winner's
registration are one transition, so _register_client carries the reason the
connect itself ended the previous session onto the record it writes, and the
index shows connected: true with disconnectReason: DUPLICATE_CLIENTID — the
reason describes how the current state came about. An ordinary reconnect
carries nothing and clears the older reason, because that disconnect was a
transition of its own that the new connect supersedes. Without this the
value was unobservable through any surface: disconnect_reason() documented a
DUPLICATE_CLIENTID no caller could ever read.

Connectivity is not persisted, and get_state / restore_state / broker_reset
leave it out: no session survives a restart, so restoring a thing as
connected would put a claim in the index that the broker cannot back.

Part of #1343.

fix(s3): compute CRC64NVME checksums instead of refusing them (#1389)

CRC-64/NVME is the algorithm current AWS SDKs and the CLI checksum
uploads with by default, and PutObject answered it with InvalidRequest on
the grounds that it needs a native CRC library. A stock `aws s3 cp` or
`aws s3api put-object` therefore failed before it began, unless the caller
knew to set AWS_REQUEST_CHECKSUM_CALCULATION=when_required.

The algorithm is plain arithmetic -- the reflected form of polynomial
0xAD93D23594C93659 with all-ones init and xorout -- so compute it from a
byte-at-a-time table in the stdlib, adding no dependency. PutObject and
CopyObject now validate a client-supplied x-amz-checksum-crc64nvme
(BadDigest on mismatch), and Get/HeadObject return it under
x-amz-checksum-mode: ENABLED. The tests pin the result to the algorithm's
published check value, b"123456789" -> 0xAE8B14860A799888, and to a
bit-at-a-time reference rather than to the table itself.

CRC32C still requires the native google-crc32c and is still refused.

fix(ec2): emit the public address under the real wire tags, and generate valid ones (#1424)

DescribeInstances and RunInstances wrote the public address as

    <publicDnsName>...</publicDnsName>
    <publicIpAddress>...</publicIpAddress>

but the EC2 query protocol names those members dnsName and ipAddress.
botocore's ec2-2016-11-15 model is explicit:

    PublicDnsName    locationName = dnsName
    PublicIpAddress  locationName = ipAddress

An SDK drops members it cannot map, silently, so every instance came back
without PublicIpAddress and PublicDnsName even though the server had generated
both. On boto3 against a stock server:

    run_instances(...); describe_instances(...)
    PublicIpAddress present: False
    PublicDnsName   present: False
    PrivateIpAddress: 10.0.212.225      <- the correctly-tagged control

Any code that waits for an address, or feeds one to SSH or a health check,
sees nothing to wait for.

Fixing the tags made a second defect reachable, so it is fixed here too rather
than shipped into view. _random_ip appended exactly two octets regardless of
its prefix, which suits "10.0." and not "52.":

    _random_ip("10.0.") -> 10.0.104.37     four octets
    _random_ip("52.")   -> 52.55.218       three

AllocateAddress has been returning that shape as PublicIp on every release,
where it is already visible to callers: ipaddress.ip_address("52.55.218")
raises. The generator now completes any prefix to four octets, so both the
instance addresses this commit exposes and the elastic IPs that were already
exposed parse.

Tests: tests/test_ec2.py gains the SDK round-trip for both instance fields
(with an ipaddress parse, since presence alone was never the whole claim) and
an AllocateAddress/DescribeAddresses validity check. Both fail on the current
code, the first on the missing field and the second on the malformed one.
155 passed.

feat(iot-jobs-data): AWS IoT Jobs control and data plane (#1400)

IoT device fleets are driven through Jobs, but MiniStack implemented
none of the Jobs APIs: CreateJob fell through to "Unsupported IoT path"
and the iot-jobs-data endpoint did not exist at all, so device-side
agents (OTA update loops, the AWS IoT Device SDK jobs handlers) could
not be rehearsed locally.

Implement Jobs natively: nine control-plane operations on the existing
iot service (CreateJob, DescribeJob, ListJobs, GetJobDocument,
CancelJob, DeleteJob, ListJobExecutionsForThing, DescribeJobExecution,
CancelJobExecution — URIs/methods verified against botocore's iot
service model, e.g. CreateJob is PUT /jobs/{jobId}) plus a new
iot-jobs-data device data plane (GetPendingJobExecutions,
StartNextPendingJobExecution, DescribeJobExecution incl. the $next
sentinel, UpdateJobExecution).

Job and execution state lives in services/iot.py (jobId-keyed and
(thingName, jobId)-tuple-keyed AccountRegionScopedDicts, wired into
get_state/restore_state/reset like the shadow store). Every rule of the
execution state machine lives there too, exported through that module's
public seam (jobs_pending_for_thing, jobs_start_next_execution,
jobs_describe_execution, jobs_update_execution, jobs_job_document,
parse_json_body); iot_jobs_data.py keeps no state and makes no
transition of its own — it parses, shapes, and logs, mirroring how
iot_data.py sits on the shadow store. The optimistic-concurrency and
terminal-status gates are shared by the two update paths, so those
rules exist once.

Executions walk QUEUED → IN_PROGRESS → {SUCCEEDED, FAILED, REJECTED,
CANCELED}: versionNumber bumps on every transition and a stale
expectedVersion is rejected with a 409 carrying the current version.
A non-continuous job auto-COMPLETEs with jobProcessDetails counts once
every execution is terminal — and not before, so a two-thing fleet
stays IN_PROGRESS until the second device reports. SNAPSHOT jobs
resolve thing-group membership once at creation; CONTINUOUS jobs
re-resolve lazily on read, natively against the _thing_groups store.

Creation validates against exactly what the resolver can reach, so a
job that is accepted is a job that can finish. One function resolves a
target ARN, and CreateJob rejects (ResourceNotFoundException, as AWS
does) anything it answers nothing for: another service, another
account, another region, or an unknown thing / thing group. Gating on
the ARN's resource segment alone would take a cross-region target,
resolve it to zero executions, and leave a job stuck IN_PROGRESS that
only force can delete. jobId is validated on the JobId pattern both
service models declare ([a-zA-Z0-9_-], max 64) rather than the wider
thing-name one — a jobId carrying a `:` is unreachable for the device
that has to ask for it by id — and targetSelection has to be one of
the two modeled values instead of being stored verbatim, where any
unknown string quietly read as "not CONTINUOUS".

Deleting a thing deletes its job executions and re-runs the completion
check on each affected job. An execution left behind for a thing that
no longer exists is non-terminal forever: nobody can report on it, so
its job never reaches COMPLETED, the store keeps growing, and a new
thing registered under the same name inherits the dead one's in-flight
rollout. That is also why the completion check treats "no executions
left" as complete — every path into it materializes first, so an empty
list means the last execution was swept, not that the job has yet to
start.

Records store epoch milliseconds; the control plane emits epoch-seconds
floats (timestamp shapes) while the data plane emits millisecond longs,
matching the two service models.

Routing: iot-jobs-data is registered in SERVICE_REGISTRY and in
SERVICE_PATTERNS ahead of iot-data/iot, since its host also matches the
iot regex. The host pattern covers both spellings — the
{prefix}.jobs.iot.{region} endpoint DescribeEndpoint(endpointType=
"iot:Jobs") advertises and the {prefix}.data.jobs.iot.{region} one the
Device SDK documents; matching only the latter sent a device following
the documented flow to the control plane, where GET /things/{t}/jobs is
a different operation (ListJobExecutionsForThing) answering a different
envelope. The control plane recognizes its own /things/{name}/jobs
routes by partitioning the path instead of matching a bare "jobs"
substring, so a thing literally named "jobs" keeps its CRUD routes. The
SDK's iot-jobs-data credential scope resolves via the early return.

Deliberate divergences from AWS, each pinned by a test:

  * documentSource is NOT fetched. AWS serves the S3 object's content
    as the job document; here a documentSource job gets a
    {"documentSource": "<url>"} placeholder instead, so the execution
    lifecycle still runs end to end. Pass `document` when the content
    matters.
  * executionNumber is write-once (always 1). AWS increments it when an
    execution is retried; nothing re-queues an execution here, so only
    versionNumber carries concurrency.
  * TIMED_OUT and REMOVED are recognized as terminal and counted in
    jobProcessDetails, but nothing sets them — there are no execution
    timeouts, and a deleted thing's executions are deleted with it
    rather than marked REMOVED.
  * The stale-expectedVersion error code differs by plane, following
    each service model rather than the API reference: the iot model
    declares VersionConflictException for CancelJobExecution, but the
    iot-jobs-data model declares only InvalidStateTransitionException
    for UpdateJobExecution. Returning the unmodeled code on the device
    plane makes a device's `except
    client.exceptions.VersionConflictException` raise AttributeError
    instead of catching, because botocore only synthesizes exception
    classes for the errors its model lists.

Part of #1343 (§2.2).

Validation (pytest against a local ministack via MINISTACK_ENDPOINT;
test_iot_jobs + test_iot + test_router + test_persistence together:
677 passed, 0 failed). Two deliberate pins beyond the lifecycle suite:
a white-box test seeds restored TIMED_OUT/REMOVED executions and asserts
they are counted in jobProcessDetails and complete the job (nothing local
sets those statuses, but a restored record must still behave), and a wire
test pins that ListJobs / ListJobExecutionsForThing serve one unbounded
page with no nextToken, matching the docstrings that now disclose it.

  ruff check clean on iot.py, iot_jobs_data.py, router.py, and the
  touched test modules.

fix(cfn): apply AWS::IoT::Policy updates instead of rolling the stack… (#1406)

* fix(cfn): apply AWS::IoT::Policy updates instead of rolling the stack back

A stack update fell through to create for want of an update handler and hit
ResourceAlreadyExistsException on its own policy. A changed PolicyDocument now
becomes the new default policy version; a changed PolicyName replaces the
policy.

* fix(cfn): prune AWS::IoT::Policy versions to stay under the five-version cap

IoT keeps at most five versions of a policy and CreatePolicyVersion answers

update path now prunes the same way, keeping the version list the shape it

CloudFormation: support API Gateway (v1) API keys and usage plans (#1425)

AWS::ApiGateway::ApiKey, AWS::ApiGateway::UsagePlan, and
AWS::ApiGateway::UsagePlanKey failed stack creation with
"Unsupported resource type", even though the runtime CreateApiKey /
CreateUsagePlan APIs were already served.

Provision all three through those same stores:
- ApiKey supports a pinned Value, Enabled, StageKeys and CustomerId,
  updates Name/Description/Enabled in place, and exposes both Ref and

fix(s3): honor canned ACLs on buckets and key object ACLs by version (#1434)

SDKs send `put-bucket-acl --acl public-read` as an x-amz-acl header with
an empty body, and PutBucketAcl read only the body, so the canned grant
vanished and the bucket read back owner-only.  A caller that gates
anonymous access on the reported grants -- S3Proxy's aws-s3 backend
among them -- then treated every bucket as private.  CreateBucket
dropped the header the same way.  Both now validate the canned value and
store the grants it implies through the object-side table (#1322),
log-delivery-write included; an XML body must be well-formed
(MalformedACLError) and a request with neither header nor body answers
MissingSecurityHeader, as on AWS.

Object ACLs are now keyed per version like tags (#1058): ?versionId=
reads or writes that version's ACL, a fresh version starts from the
default policy instead of inheriting its predecessor's, and the canned
value on PutObject sticks to the version that PUT created.  Version and
bucket deletes drop the stored entries.  The browser-POST form names its
field `acl` rather than `x-amz-acl`, so it never matched the synthetic
header list and was discarded; it now applies to the uploaded object.

This is thirteen fewer failures on S3Proxy's s3-tests lane: the twelve
ACL-cluster tests pass, and test_expected_bucket_owner returns to being
an honest expected failure instead of passing by accident off the
dropped grant.

fix(s3): honor If-Match and If-None-Match on CompleteMultipartUpload (#1435)

Conditional writes landed on PutObject, but CompleteMultipartUpload
accepted the same headers and ignored them: a create-once
(If-None-Match: *) or compare-and-swap (If-Match: <etag>) upload that
took the multipart path silently overwrote whatever was at the key.
The complete now evaluates the same preconditions PutObject does --
_check_put_preconditions against the current object at complete time,
after the upload-id checks so NoSuchUpload keeps precedence, and after
the idempotent replay, which deliberately bypasses them because the
original request already passed its conditions when it committed.

Holding the shared helper against ceph/s3-tests also settled its one
divergence: If-Match: * against a missing key answered the RFC 7232
412, but AWS documents a single If-Match error row for a key with no
current object -- 404 NoSuchKey -- and s3-tests pins that for the "*"
form and the ETag form alike, on PutObject and on the multipart
complete.  Both operations now answer 404 there, and the test that
pinned the 412 now pins the documented answer.

This fixes the three multipart conditional-write tests on S3Proxy's
s3-tests lane, tests LocalStack fails as well.

fix(s3): versioning edge cases — the null version, marker signals, versioned copies (#1436)

Five behaviors around the edges of object versioning now match AWS.

A PUT on a Suspended bucket minted a fresh UUID version id exactly like
an Enabled one; S3 stores that write as the "null" version -- replacing
any previous null version -- and answers without x-amz-version-id, which
is what happens now, on PutObject, POST, CopyObject and
CompleteMultipartUpload alike.  A suspended DELETE mints its marker
under the literal "null" id the same way.  The object written before
versioning was enabled used to vanish from the version index at the
first versioned overwrite; it now stays addressable as VersionId=null
and becomes current again when the newer version is deleted.

Delete markers announce themselves: DeleteObjects without a per-key
VersionId on a versioned bucket now creates a marker -- for keys that
never existed too -- and reports DeleteMarker/DeleteMarkerVersionId on
the Deleted entry, and a GET/HEAD 404 for a key hidden by a marker
carries x-amz-delete-marker: true with the marker's id.

UploadPartCopy ignored the copy source's ?versionId= and copied the
current bytes; it now copies that exact version and echoes
x-amz-copy-source-version-id.  A versioned CopyObject dropped the source
version's user metadata -- the index kept it, the synthesized source
object just didn't carry it.  And both copy operations percent-decoded
the copy-source header before splitting at "?", so a key legitimately
named "?versionId" -- which arrives encoded -- read as an empty key with
a version qualifier; the raw header is split first now.

The five version-minting sites shared five hand-copied bookkeeping
blocks; they now go through one _record_object_version helper, which is
what makes the null-version rules uniform, and the "null" special-case
in version deletes only addresses a current object that actually is the
null version instead of purging whatever is there.

This fixes eleven versioning tests on S3Proxy's s3-tests lane and lets
test_multipart_copy_versioned rejoin the run -- its failure mode was
what made pytest diff two multi-megabyte bodies.

fix(cfn): preserve the uniqueness suffix when truncating auto-generated physical names (#1429)

_physical_name() built the full "{stack}-{logicalId}-{suffix}" string and
only then sliced it to max_len from the end. For a deeply-nested CDK stack,
the nested stack's own generated name (parent name + nested-stack logical
id + a CloudFormation-assigned suffix) can already exceed a downstream
resource's own name-length limit on its own — e.g. Lambda's 64-char
FunctionName cap. When that happens, every resource in that nested stack
truncates to an identical string regardless of logical_id, since the part
that would have disambiguated them (logical_id, then the hash) never
survives the slice.

Concretely: every Lambda function inside such a nested stack collapsed onto
one physical function, so only one of them ever actually ran regardless of
which the caller invoked — surfaced as every route on an HttpApi returning
the same handler's response, no matter the path or method.

Now reserves room for the suffix and truncates the "{stack}-{logicalId}-"
prefix instead, so the one part that actually guarantees uniqueness (a
hash of stack_name *and* logical_id) always survives. No change in shape

fix(dsql): enforce the locking clause DSQL enforces, not the predicate (#1442)

Strict mode rejected `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` unless the query was a single
table with an equality on every primary key column. The check compared the
WHERE clause's column against the key name as raw SQL text, so `WHERE "id" =
$1` did not match key column `id`. Any client that quotes its identifiers
therefore failed every locking read, with a message that blamed the schema.

Measuring against a live cluster (eu-central-1, 2026-08-18, server_version
16.15) showed the rule itself is obsolete. DSQL restricts the lock strength,
not the predicate: FOR UPDATE locks whatever the query selects — no WHERE
clause, a non-key column, an inequality, IN/OR, a join, or a table with no
primary key all succeed, as do NOWAIT, SKIP LOCKED and OF — while FOR NO KEY
UPDATE, FOR SHARE and FOR KEY SHARE are refused with

  0A000: locking clauses other than FOR UPDATE/FOR KEY SHARE are not supported

at any nesting depth, a CTE or subquery included.

So the predicate rule is gone and a lock-strength rule takes its place. It is
token-based (FOR SHARE inside a string literal is text, not a clause) and
needs no catalog probe, so a locking read is forwarded without a round-trip.
The rule is syntactic where DSQL's is planner-level: a share clause that
cannot reach a relation, or that a stronger clause on the same relation
supersedes, is a no-op that DSQL accepts and this refuses — documented in the
module's limitations.

Two identifier bugs of the same class went with it. `ALTER TABLE ... DROP
COLUMN "ID"` was read as key column `id` and refused, and the primary-key
probe stripped the quotes from its relation name, so `"myschema".t` became
`myschema".t` and resolved to nothing while a table created as `"MyTable"`
case-folded to `mytable` and was not found, silently disabling the rule.
Identifiers are now folded the way the server folds them (bare to lower case,
quoted verbatim, "" unescaped) and the relation is requoted part by part
before the lookup.

Verified against the same cluster: an 80-case matrix over the quoting,
qualification and predicate forms agrees with the service exactly, sqlstates
included, and an 18-case probe agrees on message text too, with the single
documented no-op divergence. 58 tests added.

fix(s3): state, validate, and enforce server-side encryption (#1439)

SSE-S3, SSE-KMS and SSE-C headers all returned 200 and were then
forgotten: nothing was echoed on the PUT reply or on later reads, an
object written under a customer key read back without one, and
incoherent requests -- a wrong key MD5, key material without the
algorithm, SSE-C combined with KMS -- were accepted.

MiniStack still does not encrypt at rest.  Like the ACL plane, SSE is
contract state now: validated on write (InvalidArgument on a bad
algorithm, a non-256-bit key, a missing or mismatched key MD5, mutually
exclusive modes together, or aws:kms naming no key -- there is no
implicit account aws/s3 key to fall back to), persisted with the object
so HEAD and GET echo it, and enforced on reads for SSE-C, whose whole
point is that the object is unreadable without the key: a keyless read
answers 400, a wrong-key read answers 403 AccessDenied -- AWS
distinguishes the two, and LocalStack agrees -- and SSE-C parameters
offered for a plain object answer 400.  The state rides
preserved_headers, so it follows versions, copies and multipart
completes through the existing plumbing, and the customer key itself is
never stored -- only its MD5, which is all AWS keeps visible either.

A bucket's default encryption now applies to the object rather than
only stamping the PUT reply.  Multipart uploads echo their encryption
on initiate, require the initiating SSE-C key on every part and on
UploadPartCopy, and require it once more on CompleteMultipartUpload --
as AWS does and ceph/s3-tests pins -- completing into an object that
carries it.  A wrong key on a part stays 400, matching AWS's
part-specific messages.  Copies never inherit the source's encryption:
the destination's SSE comes from the copy request or the destination
bucket's default, an SSE-C source demands its key as
x-amz-copy-source-... parameters, and every response echoes what
applied.  The POST form's SSE fields work like the headers.

This fixes 100 tests on S3Proxy's s3-tests lane (16 of them jointly
with an S3Proxy-side fix: its post-copy metadata read now presents the
destination's customer key).  Two wrong-key-read tests become
deliberate divergences instead: ceph/s3-tests asserts radosgw's 400
where AWS answers 403 AccessDenied, so they are marked expected
failures for this backend as they already were for LocalStack.  The
four ?encryption-subresource tests expecting the pre-2023
ServerSideEncryptionConfigurationNotFoundError stay red deliberately:
MiniStack models the modern always-on default, as LocalStack does,
which those tests are already marked for on that backend.

fix(apigateway): route on the resource+method pair, not the resource alone (#1423)

A REST API answered 403 Missing Authentication Token for any request whose
verb the matched resource does not declare, even with a {proxy+} elsewhere in
the tree wired to serve it. Three shapes hit this, and all three are ordinary:

- an intermediate node that exists only as the parent of a deeper one, e.g.
  /jobs under /jobs/{operation_type}, declaring nothing itself
- the same node once a CORS OPTIONS preflight sits on it, which is what CDK
  and Serverless generate, so this is the common case rather than the corner
- any resource asked for a verb it does not declare

API Gateway resolves on the resource+method pair. Only an exact match keeps a
request on the specific resource; everything else falls through to the most
specific {proxy+} whose prefix matches and that serves the method.

Measured before changing anything, on real API Gateway in eu-central-1 with
MOCK integrations and no authorizer:

  GET  /jobs/reboot   200 jobs-op   exact match wins
  GET  /jobs          200 proxy     node with no methods
  POST /jobs          200 proxy     any verb
  POST /jobs/reboot   200 proxy     declared verb mismatch
  GET  /cors_only     200 proxy     OPTIONS-only node

This supersedes the 1.4.16 change that made a methodless resource answer 403.
That change was made on our own report, and the report was too narrow: we
described the methodless node because that is what we hit, and assumed a
declared resource otherwise wins. It does not.

One consequence deserves stating plainly, and it is why the last probe used a
guarded sibling rather than being reasoned about. Routing precedes
authorization, so a guarded method does not hold the path: with /admin POST at
AWS_IAM and an open {proxy+} ANY, an unsigned GET /admin is served by the
proxy. That reads like an auth bypass, and it is what the service does, so it
is what this emulates. tests/test_apigatewayv1.py pins it with the reasoning in
the docstring, because the obvious instinct is to "fix" it.

Tests: three cases in tests/test_apigatewayv1.py covering the methodless node,
the CORS-preflight-only node and the guarded sibling; each fails on the
unfixed resolver. Suite is 123 passed, with apigatewayv2, cfn and persistence
green alongside (554) since the resolver is shared.

feat(iot): MQTT over TLS on 8883, inside the iot service (#1422)

The embedded broker spoke MQTT only over WebSocket, so AWS IoT Device SDK
binaries could not connect to it: they open a TCP socket, present a client
certificate and speak MQTT directly. This adds that transport to the broker,
in iot.py next to the WebSocket path, sharing _WSSession and _feed_session so
both transports have identical packet semantics, including the
IOT_WS_FRAME_MAX_BYTES cap. The tests live with the rest of the broker in
test_iot_data.py and reuse its MQTT codec.

Configured the way the Transfer Family SFTP listener is, since the WebSocket
transport has no configuration to copy (it rides the gateway port and is
always on): on by default when cryptography is importable,
IOT_MTLS_ENABLED=0 turns it off, IOT_MTLS_PORT moves it from 8883. A port
that cannot be bound degrades to a log line rather than failing the boot.

The client certificate is optional, and what happens with it follows the rule
s3.py already applies to a presigned URL: a caller that presents no credential
is served, a caller that presents one that does not hold up is refused. No
certificate means the session runs under MINISTACK_ACCOUNT_ID, exactly like an
unsigned WebSocket upgrade. A certificate registered ACTIVE in exactly one
account serves that account and region. One that is unknown, not ACTIVE, or
ACTIVE in several accounts gets CONNACK 0x05: that reads the X.509 identity
lifecycle the registry already keeps and the control plane already enforces
(deleting an ACTIVE certificate is CertificateStateException 406), so
UpdateCertificate to INACTIVE cuts a device off as it does on AWS. The
ambiguous case cannot be attributed on the wire, since both registrations see
byte-identical bytes, so it is refused rather than awarded and the log names
both scopes.

The broker certificate is minted from the local CA and persisted with it, so a
device that pinned the chain survives restarts, and reset() rebinds the
listener with fresh material.

16 tests over private servers (default-on, disabled by env, connect without a
certificate, brokered publish, per-account delivery, deactivation cutting a
device off and reactivation restoring it, unknown and ambiguous refusals with
their log lines, registered-CA chains, reset rebind, shutdown with a device
attached).

fix(s3): carry multipart checksums through to a composite (#1453)

CreateMultipartUpload took an algorithm and forgot it, UploadPart
computed no checksum and echoed none, and the completed object carried
nothing for a read to ask about -- so a caller that uploaded with
ChecksumAlgorithm=SHA256 got a KeyError where AWS hands back a value.

Each part now stores its checksum, validated against the bytes the way
PutObject validates one, and the completion hashes the parts' digests
end to end into the composite AWS names <digest>-<parts>.  A composite
the request names must match, or the completion is a BadDigest; the
stored value reads back through ChecksumMode as COMPOSITE rather than
the FULL_OBJECT a single PUT records.

fix(dynamodb): resolve UpdateExpression aliases before the key-attribute check (#1464)

The pre-check matched key names as raw text against the UpdateExpression.
Because # and : are non-word characters, a word-boundary match on a key
named pk also matched inside the #pk alias and the :pk value reference,
so an update targeting a non-key attribute through an alias was refused
with "Cannot update attribute pk. This attribute is part of the key".

The pre-check is removed rather than replaced. _apply_update_expression
already returns updated_attrs, the alias-resolved root of every path it
touches, so the key names are tested against that set and the expression
is never scanned a second time. Error code, message and status are
unchanged.

updated_attrs is owned by _update_item and passed in, so targets resolved
before a raise survive it, and _apply_add and _apply_delete record the
path root before their operand-type checks. AWS reports the key rejection
ahead of those runtime errors, and an ADD against a key attribute hits
both.

fix(lambda): fall back to import() on ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE too (#1466)

Node's require(esm) interop throws ERR_REQUIRE_ASYNC_MODULE — a distinct
code from ERR_REQUIRE_ESM — when the required module's graph contains a
top-level await, since a synchronous require() can never wait on an async
operation. Both the warm-worker (lambda_runtime.py) and one-shot
(lambda_svc.py) Node bootstraps only caught ERR_REQUIRE_ESM, so any ESM
handler using top-level await (AWS's own documented Lambda cold-start
pattern for forcing a client connection during Init) crashed with
"Worker init failed: require() cannot be used on an ESM graph with
top-level await" instead of falling back to dynamic import() like every
other ESM handler already does.

Real AWS Lambda's runtime uses dynamic import() for ESM handlers and has
no such restriction, so this only ever broke local ministack testing.

fix(cloudformation): honor the ${!Literal} escape in Fn::Sub (#1484)

Fn::Sub treats an exclamation point after the opening brace as an
escape: ${!Literal} renders as the literal text ${Literal} with no
substitution attempted. The replacer had no case for it, so the name
missed the var map, the pseudo-parameters, the stack parameters and the
resources, and fell through to returning the name unchanged — emitting
!Literal with the braces already consumed.

An AWS::IoT::Policy pinned to ${!iot:Connection.Thing.ThingName}, the
standard way to scope a certificate to its own thing, therefore deployed
with every resource ARN reading .../client/!iot:Connection.Thing.ThingName.
That matches nothing, so the policy denied every connect, publish and
subscribe while the stack still reported CREATE_COMPLETE.

The escape is now handled before any lookup, and the dependency walker
skips escaped names so a literal ${!Foo} no longer orders the resource
against a resource named Foo.

A client sends x-amz-checksum-* to have the object checked.  Two ways
that was not happening:

A supplied value was only recomputed and compared when the request ALSO
carried x-amz-sdk-checksum-algorithm, which is not what an ordinary
precomputed-checksum PUT looks like.  Without it the value was stored
unread and echoed on every later GET and HEAD, so a corrupted body came
back wearing a checksum that had never been checked against it -- worse
than sending none, because it reads as proof.  Every supplied value is
verified now.

And a checksum sent as a trailer never arrived at all: the chunked-body
decoder stopped at the final chunk and dropped the trailing header
section on the floor, so nothing downstream could see it.  Trailing
headers are lifted into the request headers, where every reader already
looks; an explicit header still wins, since the trailer is the late
copy of the same field rather than an override.

fix(events): add the quotes an input template omits around a string variable (#1507)

AWS documents that quotes around an input-template variable holding a
string are optional: EventBridge adds them so the transformed input is
valid JSON, and adds none around a variable holding an object or array.
_apply_input_transformer pre-serialised every value and ran a flat string
replace, so the documented form {"detail": <detail>, "groupId": <groupId>}
rendered as "groupId": some-value and the target received a body that
would not parse. Consumers had to hand-quote the placeholder.

Substitution now depends on where the placeholder sits. A single regex
tokenises the template into whole string literals and placeholders; the
literal branch is tried first and consumes any escaped quote it contains,
so anything matched as a placeholder is by definition in a JSON value
position and a string there is rendered through json.dumps. Placeholders
found inside a matched literal get a second pass and interpolate raw,
because AWS does not escape a value it extracted through an input path.

Values are kept as parsed objects up to that point rather than serialised
at lookup time, which is what lets the two positions be told apart. An
object or array spliced into a string still has its internal quotes
stripped, as AWS does to keep the surrounding string valid. A template
containing no double quotes is plain text rather than JSON, so every
placeholder in it interpolates as a string and its output is unchanged;
an input path that does not resolve still yields an empty string.

fix(s3): apply the ACL and the source conditions a copy carries (#1482)

CopyObject dropped x-amz-acl, so a copy addressed public-read landed
private and stayed that way -- the caller had no way to tell except by
reading the ACL back.  It now permissions the destination as a put
does, and refuses an unknown value rather than ignoring it.  A copy
without one leaves the destination private rather than inheriting
whatever the key it replaced carried.

UploadPartCopy ignored all four x-amz-copy-source-if-* headers and
copied the range regardless, which is the hazard a conditional read
exists to prevent: the part is assembled from a source that has since
changed.  CopyObject already judged them correctly, so the block moves
into a helper both operations ask -- one place to be right, and no
chance of the two drifting apart.

fix(s3): answer the versioning edges the way S3 answers them (#1483)

Four places where a versioned bucket answered something other than what
AWS says, all of them found by s3proxy's conformance tests:

- DeleteBucket emptied a bucket that still held versions.  Deleting an
  object under versioning writes a delete marker rather than removing
  anything, so a bucket whose listing is empty may still hold every
  version ever written to it; AWS refuses it BucketNotEmpty until they
  go by version id, and dropping them silently loses data the caller
  could otherwise still read.

- Reading a delete marker by its version id returned 200 with an empty
  body on GET, and NoSuchVersion on HEAD.  The marker is there and has
  no content, which AWS says with 405 and the marker's own headers;
  neither of the old answers told the caller which of the two it was.

- An ACL or tag op naming a version that never existed, or that has
  since been deleted, read back the default policy as though the
  version were merely unpermissioned.  A version id addresses a version
  the way a key addresses an object: what is not there answers
  NoSuchVersion.  All five subresource ops ask the one helper.

- ListObjectVersions ignored the delimiter and listed every key flat,
  so a client walking a versioned bucket by folder saw no groups at
  all.  It now rolls up exactly as ListObjects does.

fix(pipes): deliver DynamoDB stream records to a Step Functions target (#1521)

The poller delivered to SNS and to nothing else, so a pipe whose target was a
state machine reported RUNNING, advanced no stream position and moved no
records, with no error and no log line.

A states target now gets one StartExecution per batch, carrying the records as
the JSON array $states.input reads, which is the shape Pipes delivers on AWS.

A pipe's stream position advances only once the whole batch has reached its
target. A StartExecution that fails and a target this poller cannot serve both
leave the records on the stream for the next poll to retry, and log a warning
naming the pipe.

CloudFormation: fail loudly on undeletable resources + in-place update handlers (#1534)

* fix(cloudformation): fail loudly when a resource cannot be deleted

_delete_resource answered a missing delete handler with logger.warning and
returned as if the delete had happened. Every caller then reported success:
DeleteStack landed DELETE_COMPLETE while the resources lived on, a rollback
landed (UPDATE_)ROLLBACK_COMPLETE having undone nothing, and the resource
was silently dropped from the stack record either way. Of the 132 types in
_RESOURCE_HANDLERS, five had a create handler but no delete.

- _delete_resource now raises ValueError for a type without a delete
  handler. The intentionally stateless internal family keeps its silent
  path: unregistered AWS::CloudFormation::* types never provisioned
  anything real, and the registered WaitCondition / WaitConditionHandle
  get an explicit no-op delete so the raise stays reserved for types that
  actually leak.
- AWS::Lambda::Version gets a real delete handler that removes the
  published version from the function record. Its physical id is now the
  qualified version ARN (arn:...:function:name:1), which is what Ref
  returns on AWS - and what lets the delete find its version.
- AWS::AppSync::GraphQLSchema gets a real delete handler that removes the
  stored schema pseudo-type from the API.
- DeleteStack keeps deleting the remaining resources after a failure, then
  lands DELETE_FAILED with a stack-level event, as AWS does: the failed
  resources stay on the stack (marked DELETE_FAILED, so a retried
  DeleteStack picks them up again), everything that did delete is gone,
  and the exports stay with the still-existing stack.
- A rollback whose delete fails lands ROLLBACK_FAILED /
  UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED with a stack-level event instead of pretending
  the rollback completed.
- The update path that deletes resources removed from the template keeps
  its record-drop on failure - the behaviour we have observed on AWS is
  that the stack still lands UPDATE_COMPLETE when the cleanup phase
  cannot delete - but now logs an error and emits the resource-level
  DELETE_FAILED event it lacked.

Not covered: ContinueUpdateRollback - recovering an UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED
stack past its failed deletes is not implemented here.

Tests cover the DELETE_FAILED lifecycle (other resources deleted, failed
one retained, exports kept, retry completes), both rollback-failed states
via a custom resource that refuses its Delete, and the two new delete
handlers against externally-owned parents.

Refs:
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/APIReference/API_Stack.html
https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/aws-resource-lambda-version.html

* feat(cloudformation): in-place update handlers for the common resource types

106 of the 132 registered resource types had no update handler, so a stack
update fell through to create. For the types real templates actually update
that re-provision is destructive: a Lambda function lost its published
versions, aliases, resource policy and tags; a DynamoDB table lost its
items; an SQS queue its messages; a log group its streams; an IAM role
every policy attached from outside the template. Each type below now
updates in place through its service module's own mutation API, preserving
the physical id — the _iot_policy_update idiom.

- AWS::Lambda::Function - UpdateFunctionCode + UpdateFunctionConfiguration
  (defaults mirrored from create, so a removed property reverts).
  FunctionName change replaces; a PackageType flip keeps the full
  re-provision the fallback always did (a replacement on AWS too), now
  invalidating warm workers and pooled containers the way _update_code
  does.
- AWS::DynamoDB::Table - UpdateTable for billing mode, throughput, stream
  spec, SSE, deletion protection, and GSI reconciliation (one action per
  call, as on AWS). KeySchema / LSI stay create-only, following the
  registry: a change extends the existing custom-named-replacement
  refusal; an auto-named table is re-created.
- AWS::ApiGateway::RestApi / Resource / Method / Stage - patch-in-place
  for the mutable fields; Resource (all of whose properties are
  create-only) replaces; a changed RestApi Body re-imports as a
  replacement (no local PutRestApi). Deployment stays create-only: AWS
  treats a deployment as an immutable snapshot.
- AWS::IoT::TopicRule - ReplaceTopicRule semantics via put_topic_rule,
  keeping createdAt.
- AWS::SNS::Topic - DisplayName plus reconciliation of the template's
  inline Subscription list. Inline-created records carry a private
  marker, so the reconcile can never remove a standalone
  AWS::SNS::Subscription (or a plain Subscribe) that happens to share
  protocol and endpoint.
- AWS::SQS::Queue - SetQueueAttributes semantics; messages survive.
- AWS::Logs::LogGroup - retention; streams survive.
- AWS::S3::BucketPolicy - policy document rewrite on the same bucket.
- AWS::IAM::Role - assume-role document, description, session duration,
  ManagedPolicyArns and inline Policies reconciled by diff, so
  attachments made outside the stack survive. Deleting a role now
  detaches its managed policies first, keeping AttachmentCount honest.
- AWS::IAM::ManagedPolicy - a changed PolicyDocument becomes a new
  default policy version on the same ARN (pruning the oldest non-default
  version at the five-version cap, like the CloudFormation handler),
  via a new iam.detach_managed_policy twin for the attach helper. A Path
  or Description change is a replacement; under an unchanged custom name
  it is refused, as real CloudFormation refuses it.

Name changes (and the other genuinely create-only identity properties)
replace via create-new-then-delete-old, matching CloudFormation's
replacement order; the shared _rename_replacement helper carries that
prologue for the name-keyed handlers.

One test per handler: deploy, update a mutable property, assert the
physical id survived and the new value - plus the state a re-create
would have destroyed - through the service API. A rename-replacement
test covers the create-new-then-delete-old path, and a standalone
subscription is pinned to survive the inline reconcile.

https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AWSCloudFormation/latest/UserGuide/aws-resource-dynamodb-table.html

fix(iot): publish shadow notifications for HTTP data-plane updates (#1531)

An HTTP UpdateThingShadow stored the state and emitted nothing, so a topic
rule on shadow/update/accepted fired for MQTT updates but never for HTTP
ones. On AWS accepted/delta/documents are state-change notifications the
Device Shadow service emits however the update arrived. The MQTT bridge's
success emission moves into a shared helper; the HTTP path snapshots
pre/post documents the same way and awaits it, and an HTTP delete publishes
delete/accepted. An HTTP get stays silent (get/accepted is the MQTT
response channel) and HTTP failures publish no rejected envelope.

feat(iot): provisioning-template control plane + AWS::IoT::ProvisioningTemplate (#1532)

Neither existed: the control plane answered "Unsupported IoT path" and the
CloudFormation type rolled back every stack that carried one. Storage + CRUD
only — no fleet-provisioning MQTT workflow; provisioningRoleArn is
presence-checked, consistent with the no-IAM-validation posture elsewhere.
The provisioner drives the real API and replaces on a TemplateName change
the way AWS::IoT::Policy does.

feat(apigateway): route the data plane through registered custom domains (#1533)

The domain and base-path-mapping control plane existed, but no request ever
consulted it: a custom-domain host fell through host-pattern guessing into S3
(or a wrong service when the name contained a token like "iot."). Requests now
resolve registered domains before any guessing - longest base path wins,
"(none)" (or an explicit empty basePath) is the root mapping, and a mapping
that names a stage is authoritative while a stage-less mapping takes the
stage from the remaining path, like a plain execute-api URL. The Host lookup
ignores case, and an OPTIONS preflight to a registered domain flows through
the API's own corsConfiguration instead of the generic wildcard preflight.
Unregistered hosts keep the existing fallthrough; the cost is a linear scan
over the registered domain names for dotted-host requests that match no
execute-api pattern.

feat(iot): deliver IoT Jobs over MQTT (#1535)

The jobs data plane existed only over HTTP; nothing was published on
$aws/things/<t>/jobs/#, so a device firmware speaking the AWS Jobs MQTT
contract hung forever on notify-next. The reserved request topics (get,
start-next, <jobId>/get incl. the documented $next sentinel, <jobId>/update)
now answer on their accepted/rejected topics from the same store the HTTP
plane uses — jobDocument as a JSON object, rejections as the string
ErrorCode enum with executionState on version/state conflicts — and
notify/notify-next fire on create, cancel, delete, and terminal reports:
notify whenever the pending set's membership changes, notify-next only when
the job at its front changes, and neither on start-next (QUEUED ->
IN_PROGRESS keeps the execution pending and first; verified against a live
device capture). Mirrors the shadow bridge (parser recursion guard
included); CreateJob and the cancel/delete handlers become async the way
_register_certificate did, and the device-plane execution view is lifted so
both planes and the bridge share one shape.

Behaviour fix riding along: the shared view emits whole epoch seconds,
which the HTTP iot-jobs-data plane had wrong all along — it served the
records' raw milliseconds, while the API reference words every JobExecution
stamp as "The time, in seconds since the epoch" (and a live capture agrees,
all 10-digit values). Records keep millisecond resolution internally so
same-second executions still hand out in queue order.

Boundaries: lazy CONTINUOUS materialization on reads does not notify;
DeleteThing's execution sweep does not notify the deleted thing (the sweep
is itself a divergence — AWS keeps a deleted thing's executions, so it
publishes nothing there either); stepTimeoutInMinutes and executionNumber
request members are accepted but ignored.

An awsvpc task gets its own network namespace — an ENI on Fargate — so its

container port 80 under awsvpc — the shape a Terraform ECS + ALB module produces —
could therefore never both run.

fix(ecs): register a service's tasks in its target groups (#1550)

* fix(ecs): register a service's tasks in its target groups

An ECS service created with a loadBalancers block stored it and never acted on it,
so nothing was ever registered with the target group. DescribeTargetHealth returned
an empty list and every request through the load balancer fell through to the
listener's default action, which reads as the ALB data plane being unimplemented —
it isn't. dispatch_request, rule matching and _proxy_http_target all work; they just
had no targets to forward to.

A service now reconciles the membership of the target groups it names, from the
addresses of its running tasks. Membership is replaced wholesale rather than tracked
as add/remove events, which makes it correct for scale-up, scale-in, task
replacement and service deletion alike, and idempotent if it runs twice.

Task addresses were not recorded anywhere, so an awsvpc task now carries its address
the way real ECS reports it — attachments[].details[privateIPv4Address] — which is
where both a target group and DescribeTasks look for it.

* fix(ecs): serialise target-group publication, and select tasks by group

Review feedback on #1550.

Selecting a service's tasks by startedBy differed from the predicate
_reconcile_service_tasks uses for its own recount, which is `group`. Both are set
by that function today, so the sync did find its tasks — but the two could
disagree for a task created any other way, and the registered targets would then
contradict the runningCount reported beside them. Now both use `group`.

Collecting the addresses and publishing them is a read-modify-write on shared
state, and handlers no longer run serialised on the event loop, so two
reconciliations could interleave: one samples the tasks before a scale-in and
publishes after it, re-registering the tasks the scale-in removed. It is now done
under resource_lock, with no Docker call or re-entrant dispatch inside the lock,
per the rule in ministack.core.concurrency.

Tests:
  - test_ecs_sync_service_targets_selects_tasks_by_group pins the predicate,
    including a task carrying the group but no startedBy.
  - test_ecs_sync_service_targets_does_not_publish_a_stale_view stalls one
    reconcile between sampling and publishing while a second one scales in. It
    fails without the lock with the pre-scale-in targets still registered.

fix(elbv2): read rule conditions sent as a typed config (#1551)

* fix(elbv2): read rule conditions sent as a typed config

A listener rule condition carries its values either in the flat legacy Values list
or in a per-field typed config — PathPatternConfig, HostHeaderConfig,
HttpRequestMethodConfig, SourceIpConfig. Only the flat form was parsed, so a rule
created by the Terraform AWS provider — which sends the typed form — was stored with
an empty Values list.

An empty condition matches nothing, so the rule never fired and every request fell
through to the listener's default action. With a fixed-response default that reads
as the load balancer ignoring its rules; with two services behind one listener
routed by path, neither is reachable.

Conditions are now read from whichever shape the caller used, preferring the flat
list so existing behaviour is untouched. Tests cover both.

Found running a Terraform ECS + ALB service pair against MiniStack.

* fix(elbv2): answer rule conditions in both shapes, not just the flat list

Follow-up to the parsing fix in this branch. Storing the values was only half of
it: DescribeRules rendered nothing but the flat <Values> list, and AWS answers with
that *and* the per-field typed config carrying the same values.

The Terraform provider reads the typed config for path_pattern and host_header, so
it saw an empty condition on every read and planned a change on every run to put
the values back — a permanent diff on an unchanged configuration, which is how the
gap actually shows up in use.

Conditions are now rendered in both shapes, and the round-trip is asserted for
path-pattern, host-header and http-request-method.

fix: six fields accepted on write but never reported on read (#1558)

* fix(lambda): return EventSourceMappingArn on event source mappings

ListTags already accepts an ESM ARN, but nothing hands that ARN to the caller:
CreateEventSourceMapping, Get and List all omit EventSourceMappingArn. The
Terraform provider reads the field off the mapping and calls ListTags with it,
so with the field absent it reads no tags at all and every plan shows a tag
diff on every mapping.

The existing coverage missed this because it builds the ARN by hand, which a
real client cannot do. The new test asserts the ARN is present on all three
read paths and that the value returned is the one ListTags accepts.

Derived in _esm_response rather than stored on the record so mappings created
before this — restored state included — report it too.

* fix(s3control): wrap ListTagsForResource tags in <Tag>, not <member>

s3control's TagList declares locationName "Tag", so AWS returns
<Tags><Tag>..</Tag></Tags>. The handler emitted <member> wrappers instead.
boto3 tolerates that, which is why the existing tests pass; aws-sdk-go-v2
does not, and parses an empty tag list. Terraform therefore refreshes an
S3 bucket's tags_all to empty and plans the same tag change forever, and
applying it does not settle.

emitting <member>. The new test asserts on the wire format, since a
boto3-level assertion cannot distinguish the two.

* fix(kinesis): echo KeyId alongside EncryptionType

StartStreamEncryption stored KeyId but no describe path returned it, so an
encrypted stream reported kms_key_id as empty and Terraform planned to set it
on every run. Added to both StreamDescription and StreamDescriptionSummary,
and omitted entirely when the stream is unencrypted, as AWS does.

* fix(rds): keep ServerlessV2ScalingConfiguration and the PI retention period

Two fields were dropped on read:

ServerlessV2ScalingConfiguration was never parsed, stored or serialised, so
serverlessv2_scaling_configuration read back empty on an Aurora Serverless v2
cluster. It is emitted only when a bound was supplied, so a provisioned
cluster does not gain an empty block.

PerformanceInsightsRetentionPeriod was hardcoded to 7 on the record and then
never serialised at all, so the provider read 0. It now honours the requested
value and appears in the instance response.

* fix(cognito): keep UserAttributeUpdateSettings and a disabled software-token MFA config

Two more fields a user pool accepted but never reported.

UserAttributeUpdateSettings was neither stored on CreateUserPool nor listed as
updatable, so it read back absent and Terraform proposed the same block on
every plan.

GetUserPoolMfaConfig dropped SoftwareTokenMfaConfiguration when it was falsy.
A caller turning software-token MFA off sends an empty object — `enabled =
false` serialises with the false field omitted — so the config it had just set
came back missing and the change was re-sent forever. An explicitly set config
is now reported with Enabled normalised to a boolean, while one that was never
set stays absent, which is what keeps an unset field from reading as drift.
Both the getter and the setter render this block and now agree.

fix(ecs): relaunch a restored service's tasks (#1557)

restore_state marks every restored task STOPPED, because its container went
with the process that ran it, and nothing then reconciles the services. A
restarted ministack therefore reports each service's persisted runningCount
while no container exists, and a load balancer in front of it keeps forwarding
to addresses nothing is listening on — the service looks healthy and every
request fails. Recovering needed a manual force-new-deployment.

Real ECS relaunches: keeping desiredCount satisfied is the service scheduler's
whole job. ACTIVE services are now reconciled once after a restore, on a daemon
thread so pulling images does not block startup behind the Docker daemon
(ECS_RESTORE_RECONCILE_DELAY_SECONDS, default 2). A service that cannot be
relaunched is logged and skipped so one unreachable image cannot strand the
rest.

The relaunch hangs off the module's import-time restore, and ECS is otherwise
imported lazily on the first ECS request — so a workload that only reaches its
service through a load balancer never triggered it. ECS joins the boot
eager-load list next to RDS, which respawns its persisted containers for the
same reason, guarded on persisted services existing so stacks without them pay
no cold-start cost.

feat(kms): add GenerateRandom (#1536)

fix: run Lambda functions and ECS tasks on the architecture they declare (#1561)

* fix(lambda): run a function on the architecture it declares

The container was created without a platform, so Docker used the host's
architecture regardless of what Architectures said. An arm64 function on an
x86_64 host ran as x86_64.

That is invisible until a layer carries a native wheel. The handler then fails
at import naming the library rather than the mismatch — psycopg reports "no pq
wrapper available", which reads as a missing dependency, not as a function
running on the wrong architecture. It cost a full CI debugging cycle to find.

The declared architecture is now passed to Docker. A cached image of the wrong
architecture is treated as absent and re-pulled for the right platform, since
Docker would otherwise refuse to start it and the refusal would surface as an
opaque run error instead of a pull.

Set before the LAMBDA_DOCKER_FLAGS merge, so an explicit --platform there still
wins.

* fix(ecs): run a task on the architecture its task definition declares

runtimePlatform was stored when a task definition was registered and never read
again — one mention in the whole file. Docker therefore chose the host's
architecture, and an ARM64 task definition on an x86_64 host started a container
that could not execute its own entrypoint.

It failed quietly. Creating the container is the part that succeeds, so the task
reported as started and ECS logged "started container"; the only symptom was a
service that never answered. That is the same shape as the Lambda bug in the
previous commit: a declared architecture accepted, echoed back so Terraform sees
no drift, and ignored at the one moment it decides anything.

A task definition with no runtimePlatform is left alone rather than pinned to
the host explicitly, so existing single-architecture setups are unaffected.
