fix(s3): stop sending s3:TestEvent to Lambda notification targets (#1688)

PutBucketNotificationConfiguration fanned the s3:TestEvent out to every destination in the config, Lambda included. AWS sends it to SQS queues and SNS topics only.

The PutBucketNotificationConfiguration API reference draws the distinction: S3 "verifies that any Amazon SNS or SQS destination exists, and that the bucket owner has permission to publish to it by sending a test notification. In the case of AWS Lambda destinations, Amazon S3 verifies that the Lambda function permissions grant Amazon S3 permission to invoke the function from the Amazon S3 bucket." A permission check, not an invocation. The same page's atomicity note is explicit that for a config holding SNS, SQS and Lambda targets, "Amazon S3 sends test messages to your SNS topic".

The test payload has no Records array, so an S3-triggered handler that indexes into it raises. Delivery runs through invoke_async_with_retry, which retries to MaximumRetryAttempts (default 2, so three attempts) and then routes the exhausted event to the function's DLQ or DestinationConfig.OnFailure target. The cost is not only the error traces on every deploy: a synthetic event that AWS never sends lands in the dead-letter queue, indistinguishable from a genuinely dropped message. Any CDK stack with an S3-triggered Lambda reaches this through BucketNotificationsHandler.

This reverses the Lambda half of #416, which quoted the paragraph above but stopped one sentence short of the Lambda case.

Queue and topic destinations are unaffected, and real object events still invoke the function; the new test asserts both.

fix(lambda): run durable invocations on the warm pool (#1703)

A durable invocation of a python or nodejs function went to the one-shot
executor: the three AWS_LAMBDA_DURABLE_* variables differ per call and a
pooled worker's environment is fixed at spawn time. That executor starts
a fresh interpreter and imports botocore for the invoke-depth handler on
every call, inside subprocess.run(timeout=Timeout), whose default is 3
seconds. On an idle host the round trip stays well under a second; on a
two-vCPU runner with three xdist workers it crosses the budget and every
durable invocation ends as a timeout.

The context now rides in the event under _ministack_durable_ctx, the
channel the X-Ray trace header and the invoke-depth counter already use.
Both worker bootstraps move the three variables into the environment
before the handler runs and delete them when the key is absent, so a
worker reused for a non-durable invocation does not see the previous
one's. The variable names are declared once, as the mapping the overlay
reads and the bootstraps iterate, so a fourth cannot be set by one and
left uncleared by the other. The python and nodejs arm of the dispatch
stops filtering durable invocations out of the pool. provided.* keeps
the one-shot executor #1673 left it on: that arm was unconditional
before #1673, which gave the non-durable half a warm pool and kept
durable on the one shot, because a bootstrap process reads its
environment once, at spawn. The one-shot executor stays in place;
nothing reaches its python and nodejs path any more, and every other
runtime gets its mock answer before that subprocess would start.

The injection sits in the warm executor rather than in the dispatch, so
the two docker-unavailable fallbacks, which route python and nodejs to
the same pool, carry the context as well. Today they invoke the handler
with the three variables unset. The durable SDK reads its context out of
the event, which those fallbacks pass through, so nothing is lost there
today; the variables are this emulator's own convenience and they should
be set wherever the handler runs.

The dispatch tests sit next to #1673's own parametrized routing test, in
tests/test_lambda_provided_dispatch.py, so the two arms of the same
if/elif are pinned in one place.

fix(lambda): let a Node custom resource reach the CloudFormation callback in the docker executor (#1679)

The CDK bundles its own CloudFormation response submitter into every
custom-resource handler it generates (nodejs-entrypoint, the provider
framework's cfn-response, AwsCustomResource's respond). All three build
the ResponseURL PUT from the URL's hostname and path only and hand it to
https.request, so the callback goes out over TLS to port 443 whatever
the URL's scheme and port were. The local executor patches https for the
gateway host, the docker executor did not, so a Node custom resource ran
its API call and then hung its stack until ServiceTimeout with
ECONNREFUSED on port 443 of the gateway alias (the fix for #1149 rewrote
only the host, not the scheme or port).

The context shim the docker executor already injects for Node now turns
https to a gateway host (the endpoint host, host.docker.internal,
localhost, 127.0.0.1 and the host in MINISTACK_HOST, which the container
learns through _MS_GATEWAY_HOSTS) on the https default port or the
gateway port into plain http on the gateway port, with Node's default
agent. Other hosts, and gateway hosts on other ports, keep TLS. The patch
refreshes the ESM live bindings and sits in one try, so a malformed
endpoint costs the downgrade and not the function. The local executor's
own list gains the MINISTACK_HOST entry. The shim reads LAMBDA_TASK_ROOT
for the code dir (the container sets it to /var/task, so nothing changes
there) so the test can run it with node outside a container against a
local http server.

fix(s3): stop verifying a presigned URL's query-string checksum (#1705)

Since v3.729.0 the JavaScript SDK signs `x-amz-checksum-crc32` into every
presigned PutObject by default. Its value is computed over the empty body,
because whoever holds the URL picks the body later, so the parameter cannot
describe what gets uploaded.

`_merge_hoisted_amz_headers` folded every non-signing `x-amz-*` query
parameter into the headers so that a presigned upload's user metadata reaches
the handlers, and `_resolve_object_checksums` then verified the hoisted
checksum against the real body. Each behaviour is right on its own; together
they rejected with `400 BadDigest` a request real S3 answers `200`.

Exclude the five checksum value parameters from hoisting. They stay part of
the canonical request, so tampering with one still fails the signature with
`403`, but they are no longer read as a supplied integrity value. A checksum
sent as a real header is verified as before.

`x-amz-checksum-algorithm` and `x-amz-sdk-checksum-algorithm` keep hoisting.
Issue 1695 proposed excluding the latter too, but it names an algorithm for
the server to compute rather than carrying a value: it can never disagree with
a body, so it was never the reason the request was refused, and excluding it

* fix(cognito): store and return the identity pool role mappings

SetIdentityPoolRoles kept the Roles map and threw RoleMappings away, and
GetIdentityPoolRoles answered a hard-coded empty map, so a role mapping
was accepted with a 200 and then gone. Measured against a private
server, both routes lost it: a CloudFormation template declaring the
mappings on an AWS::Cognito::IdentityPoolRoleAttachment, and a plain
boto3 set_identity_pool_roles call, each read back as

  "Roles": {"authenticated": "...role/auth"}, "RoleMappings": {}

Both members are stored on the identity pool now and both come back.
The call sets the whole configuration and the API has no call that
removes a mapping on its own, so an omitted RoleMappings clears what was
there. That is reasoned from the API surface rather than measured
against a live account, and it is what the CloudFormation handler needs
to make a dropped property revert.

(RulesConfiguration required for a Rules mapping and refused for a Token
one, at most 25 rules, AmbiguousRoleResolution required for both) are
not checked, matching how the principal-tag attribute map in the same
file behaves. Credential vending is untouched and still selects the role
by authenticated or unauthenticated.

Reading the field with .get and a default keeps state written before it
existed loadable: the pool records the persistence snapshot restores,
and the pool dict the CloudFormation provisioner builds itself, carry
no entry.

* fix(cloudformation): UserPoolResourceServer updates in place

AWS::Cognito::UserPoolResourceServer had no update handler, so a stack
update fell through to the create handler. The physical id of this type
is the Identifier alone, while the record lives under the pool and the
identifier, and that combination made a pool move go wrong: measured
against a private server, repointing UserPoolId provisioned a second
resource server in the new pool and left the first one in the old pool.

its cleanup never ran. Two live resource servers for one template
resource, each serving scopes under the same identifier.

reference and now go through UpdateResourceServer on the resource server
that is already there, with a dropped Scopes back at the empty list the

leaves it off gets the identifier as MiniStack's fallback. Identifier
and UserPoolId require replacement. A changed Identifier is a rename,
which CloudFormation allows, and the new resource server is created
before the old one is removed, or left standing when the resource
carries UpdateReplacePolicy Retain: the handler deletes the predecessor
itself, in the same pass, because a pool move keeps the physical id and
the engine's cleanup would not see it. A changed UserPoolId under an
unchanged Identifier is a replacement under a custom name, which
CloudFormation refuses, and Identifier is always custom for this type:
the update now fails with the same message the other custom-named types
raise instead of moving anything.

for the template that leaves Identifier off, where the custom-name
refusal cannot fire, and takes the logical id the engine passes rather
than borrowing the physical one.

* refactor(cloudformation): one prologue and one mapping per type

The handlers this branch adds each carried their own copy of something
the file or the service already had. Four of them, no behaviour change
except where a copy was the weaker of the two.

The replacement prologue. _rename_replacement creates the replacement,
then deletes the predecessor unless the physical id came back unchanged,
because an unchanged id IS the predecessor. A subscription filter is
keyed by (group, name) and a resource server by (pool, identifier) while
both physical ids carry only the second half, so both replace under an
unchanged id and both had spelled the prologue out again, with their own
reads of the retain contextvar. They pass the pair as the identity and
ask for delete_when_id_unchanged instead. The contextvar has one reader
again, which is what it was centralised for.

The subscription filter's field mapping. It existed three times: the
create wrote the record dict inline, the update sent the same six fields
to PutSubscriptionFilter, and the service builds the record from them.
PutSubscriptionFilter creates or updates, so the create goes through it
too and _cwlogs_subfilter_payload is the one mapping. The record the
create writes is now the service's own, creationTime included.

The two policy attachments. The update was shared already; the create
and the delete were still byte-identical between the queue and the topic
version. Both go through _policy_attachment_create and
_policy_attachment_delete. AWS::S3::BucketPolicy is the third type with
the same PolicyDocument-to-JSON step and now uses the same helper, which
also drops a function-local import of a module imported at the top.

The instance profile. The provisioner minted the ARN with its own copy
of the format, its own EntityAlreadyExists guard and its own id shape
(a uuid where the service uses _gen_id("AIPA"), so one record type had
two id formats). The create calls CreateInstanceProfile now and inherits
all three; the ARN format moved into iam.instance_profile_arn, which the
service and the update handler both read. The path already carries its
own slashes, so the branch that special-cased "/" was building the same
string twice. A generated name still replaces under the same name, so
the create pops the record it is about to rewrite; a custom name gets
the service's refusal, which is what CreateInstanceProfile answers.

Part of #1601 (C1).

* refactor(cloudformation): HTTP API updates go through the service

The four HTTP API update handlers this branch adds write the service's
records by hand, while every other handler it adds calls the service
(UpdateResourceServer, PutSubscriptionFilter, UpdateAlias,
SetSubscriptionAttributes, SetIdentityPoolRoles). Their docstrings said
"as UpdateApi does" and did not call UpdateApi, so one resource ended up
with two update semantics that could only drift: the Api commit already
had to note that the service's own UpdateApi ignores description and
apiKeySelectionExpression, which the CloudFormation path writes.

The four handlers call _update_api, _update_stage, _update_integration
and _update_route now, with the same property mapping as before, so a
property the template drops still reverts to the create's default. A
non-2xx answer fails the resource rather than being discarded.

UpdateApi gains the two members it was missing, description and
apiKeySelectionExpression, and takes corsConfiguration the way the API
does: the call carries the whole configuration, so an empty one removes
it rather than storing a blank block a reader would have to interpret.
That is the CloudFormation path's behaviour moved into the service, so
both callers now get it.

One visible difference: the service pops an emptied map (requestModels,
requestParameters, requestTemplates, responseParameters) where the
create stores {}. A reader that uses .get sees the same thing, and the
popped key is what the API answers.

Part of #1601 (C1).

fix(cloudformation): UpdateReplacePolicy Retain holds for every handler-side replacement (#1701)

* fix(cloudformation): Retain holds for every handler-side replacement

The engine publishes a resource's UpdateReplacePolicy in a contextvar
around the update call, and the shared rename helper reads it before it
deletes the predecessor. 24 update handlers replace the resource
themselves without that helper, because their identity is not a single
name (a Cognito group is keyed by pool and name, a bucket policy by
bucket, a REST API resource by API and path, an event source mapping by
a generated id), and every one of them deleted the predecessor inline
without reading the policy. Measured on a private server with a template
that renames the resource under UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain: the old SSM
parameter, CloudWatch dashboard, IoT policy, Cognito user pool group and
S3 bucket policy were gone after UPDATE_COMPLETE, and because the
handler returned a new physical id the engine still recorded a
DELETE_SKIPPED event for a resource that no longer existed. One test
covered Retain on a replacement, for SQS, through the helper.

The reference: with UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain CloudFormation "keeps
the resource without deleting the resource or its contents when the
resource is replaced" and "removes it from CloudFormation's scope"
(aws-attribute-updatereplacepolicy).

Every inline predecessor delete goes through _delete_predecessor now,
which reads the contextvar and skips the delete when the template
retains the resource, and _rename_replacement does as well, so the
policy has one reader. The retaining tuple lives next to the contextvar
in provisioners.py and the engine imports it, instead of the two modules
each holding a copy.

Three handlers deleted before they created (Lambda permission, API
Gateway model, API key). They create first now, so a skipped delete
leaves a live predecessor rather than a half-replaced one. The model
handler deletes only when the (api, name) key changed, because the
emulator's CreateModel overwrites a model of the same name. An event
invoke config whose FunctionName is rewritten in another form resolves
to the same config and no longer deletes what it just wrote.

The Lambda permission's degenerate branch, where an explicit Id names
the Sid the old resource wrote, keeps its delete-then-re-put path: the
Sid cannot change, so nothing is replaced and the policy does not apply.
That branch now matches the first Sid candidate only, the one the old
resource actually used. The second is the fallback for stacks persisted
by an earlier release, and a new Id naming it is a real Sid change, so a
real replacement, which the branch used to swallow while returning the
stale physical id.

Two branches stay as they are, each with a comment: the DynamoDB
key-schema one and AWS::Location::Tracker's KmsKeyId one. The emulator's
generated name is deterministic in both, so the resource is deleted and
comes back under the same name, and the old one is lost even under
Retain, where AWS would mint a new name and keep it. A custom-named
table or tracker already refuses the replacement.

Part of #1601 (A12).

* fix(cloudformation): a nested stack's resource reads its own policy

The engine publishes a resource's UpdateReplacePolicy in a contextvar
around the update call, and every handler that replaces a resource
itself reads it there. The nested-stack deploy loop, which mirrors the
synchronous core of the engine's own loop, never set it.

So a child resource ran under whatever the parent's loop had left in the
contextvar: a parent marked Retain kept every child's predecessor
whether the child asked for it or not, and a parent without the policy
deleted the predecessor of a child that did ask. The child's own
template was never consulted.

The loop now resolves each child resource's UpdateReplacePolicy the way
the engine resolves it, with the child's parameters, conditions and
mappings, so an Fn::If works, and publishes it around that resource's
update only.

Part of #1601 (A12).

* fix(iam): one _account_from_arn, with the documented contract

iam_evaluator.py defined _account_from_arn twice at module level. Python
binds the later definition, so the copy near the condition evaluator, the
one carrying the docstring that describes what the helper refuses, was
never the one that ran: the aws:ResourceAccount resolution at its only
caller used the other.

The two contracts differ. The documented one refuses a bare "*", a value
that does not start with "arn:", and an AWS-owned ARN whose account field
holds "aws"; it accepts any other non-empty field. The one that won
refuses anything that is not twelve digits, and accepts a twelve-digit
fifth colon-separated field from a value that is not an ARN.

They are folded into one that keeps both: an account id is twelve digits,
and it is only read out of something that is an ARN. Both call sites keep
the behaviour they have today, because both pass an ARN whose account is
twelve digits, so this changes no request the emulator serves.

The parametrized test in test_iam_auth.py covered only the cases where
the two agreed, which is why the shadowing survived. It gains the two
that tell them apart: an ARN whose account field is not twelve digits,
and a twelve-digit field on a value that is not an ARN.

* test(cognito): one _NoRedirectHandler

test_cognito.py defined _NoRedirectHandler twice at module level, and the
two raise a different HTTPError. The first passes req.full_url, the URL
that was requested; the second passes newurl, the target the redirect
points at.

Which one a caller gets depends on when its opener was built.
_no_redirect_opener is built at import time, next to the first
definition, so it holds that class; _get and _post_form call
build_opener at test time, after the module finished executing, so they
get the second. Two helpers that read as the same helper report a
different HTTPError.url for the same redirect.

The first is kept. CPython's own HTTPRedirectHandler raises
HTTPError(req.full_url, ...) both when it declines a redirect and when it
detects a redirect loop, and HTTPError.url is documented as the URL of
the request that caused the error, which newurl was not: nothing was
requested from it.

No test reads url, geturl or filename off the error, so this changes no
assertion; the whole file passes unchanged.

* test(iot-jobs): one _assert_epoch_seconds

test_iot_jobs.py defined _assert_epoch_seconds twice at module level with
the same body and a shorter docstring on the second. The file grew the
duplicate when the v1.5.3 release folded test_iot_jobs_mqtt.py into it,
and the copy that survived binding is the folded one, so the docstring a
reader finds at the top of the file is not attached to the function that
runs.

The first is kept, for its docstring: it says what the assertion is for,
that a data-plane stamp is a long documented in seconds since the epoch
and that milliseconds would be off by a factor of a thousand.

* test(lambda): one import sys

test_lambda.py imports sys twice, four lines apart, the second time next to an
import shutil that sits out of order below threading. Same class as the three
shadowed definitions before it, found by the same audit, and ruff does not
flag it because I001 is not enabled on tests.

The block is sorted and the duplicate dropped. No test changes.

* test: the suite runs on a non-default GATEWAY_PORT

Eight tests asserted against a hard-coded 4566 where the value under test
was one a service had just built from GATEWAY_PORT, so the suite could
only pass on the default port.

That is the port a contributor has to move off. tests/conftest.py resets
the emulator it points at on session start, so running the suite against
the default endpoint wipes whatever is on :4566, and the way to avoid
that is a private server on another port. Then these eight fail, and
they fail looking like real regressions rather than like a harness
assumption: an ESM poller that finds no messages, an AppSync host that
does not match, a Glue container pointed at the wrong endpoint.

The five ESM tests built their queue key as an f-string. They now call
sqs._queue_url(), which is the function the poller itself calls, so the
key cannot drift from the lookup again whatever the port is. The AppSync

define it, including the EDGE_PORT fallback. Deriving it from
MINISTACK_ENDPOINT instead would agree only by coincidence, since the
two can be set independently.

Two nearby literals are deliberately left alone: the container-host test
passes its own endpoint into the helper, and the DNS-shape test sets

fix(ecs): task record and task metadata parity (#1720)

* fix(ecs): the task version counts state changes

The Task reference documents `version` as a counter a consumer compares
against the version a task state change event carries, to tell a stale copy
of the record from the current one. The emulator minted it as 1 with the task
and never moved it, so every copy compared equal and the check answered
"current" whatever had happened to the task since.

It now increments on each change of the task's own lastStatus: the move to
ACTIVATING, the move to RUNNING, and the move to STOPPED, which covers
StopTask, an essential container exiting and a start that failed. Those three
bump inside the per-task lock that already guards them. The restore after a
restart counts too, outside that lock because nothing else runs yet: it stops
every task that was running, which is exactly the change a consumer holding an
older copy needs to notice.

`_bump_task_version` sits at the top of the module next to `_attributes`, and
for the same reason: `restore_state` reaches it, and the module calls
`restore_state` at import time. Defined further down it raises NameError there,
the surrounding try/except swallows it, and all ECS state fails to restore
under PERSIST_STATE=1. There is a test that walks the AST and refuses any name
`restore_state` reaches that is defined after that call.

A real task counts the same way. A Fargate task polled through DescribeTasks
once a second reported 1 at PROVISIONING, 2 at PENDING, 3 at RUNNING, 4 when
StopTask set desiredStatus while the task was still running, 5 at
DEPROVISIONING and 6 at STOPPED; the ENI attachment moving from PRECREATED to
ATTACHING to ATTACHED did not move it. An EC2 task in bridge mode went 1 at
PENDING to 3 at RUNNING, so the state between them counts there too.

PROVISIONING and DEPROVISIONING have no counterpart here, so the number stays
below a real account's for the same task, and neither does a change below the
task: one container of several reaching RUNNING leaves it where it is. What it
promises is that it moves whenever the task's lastStatus does.

* fix(ecs): an ENI attachment belongs to an awsvpc task only

The Task reference describes `attachments` as "The Elastic Network Adapter
that's associated with the task if the task uses the `awsvpc` network mode".
A bridge or host task has no interface of its own on AWS: it shares the
container instance's, and that is where a consumer reads its address. The
emulator built the attachment for every task the moment its container reported
an address, so a bridge task described itself with an interface real ECS never
shows, and a consumer that branches on the attachment took the awsvpc path for
a task that is not on one.

Measured rather than taken from the page: a bridge task on an EC2 container
instance answers `attachments: []` and carries `containerInstanceArn` instead,
while an awsvpc task on Fargate answers one ElasticNetworkInterface.

The attachment is now built for awsvpc tasks only, and it carries the subnet
the request placed the task in next to the address. The address is recorded on
the task in every mode, under an internal key that DescribeTasks does not serve
and that the saved state drops, so the target-group sync still finds a bridge
task's address where it did before.

The first container to report an address owns it, which is what the attachment
guard used to give. A two-container awsvpc task on AWS reports one attachment,
and both containers name that same attachment id and that same private address,
so the sync must not follow a sidecar around. Each container reaches this from
its own thread, so the guard and the write it protects now share the task lock;
the docker round trip stays outside it.

The subnet is read in both casings. A service created through CloudFormation
keeps the template's `NetworkConfiguration` verbatim and replays it into
RunTask, so the SDK's casing alone would miss every CFN-defined service.

The interface id, the MAC address and the private DNS name are the other
members a real attachment carries. They are left out rather than invented,
because nothing here creates the interface they would name.

* fix(ecs): a task record has no attachmentsStatus

The task record carried `attachmentsStatus` next to its attachment. That
member does not exist on the `Task` shape. The API model carries it on
`Cluster`, where it describes the capacity providers, and nowhere else, and a
live task confirms it: neither an awsvpc task on Fargate nor a bridge task on
an EC2 container instance sends the field at any point of its lifecycle,
including while its interface is PRECREATED, ATTACHING, ATTACHED, DETACHING
and DELETED.

boto3 drops an unknown member on the way in, so this was only visible to a
client reading the wire, which is where an emulator is most often read from.

The cluster's own attachmentsStatus stays as it is. The attachment test that
asserted the member now asserts its absence.

* fix(ecs): the task metadata endpoint reports the task's status

_register_metadata wrote DesiredStatus and KnownStatus as the literal
"RUNNING" into both the task payload and the container payload, at the moment
the container was registered. The V4 endpoint then served those two strings
for the life of the task.

Before RunTask returned asynchronously the two could not disagree: the task
was RUNNING by the time the call answered, so a container that read its own
metadata could not observe anything else. The task now walks PENDING to
ACTIVATING to RUNNING with the image pull inside that window, so a container
reading ${ECS_CONTAINER_METADATA_URI_V4}/task during its own startup is told
RUNNING while DescribeTasks says otherwise, for as long as the pull takes. On
a cold image that is the longest part of the start.

Both members are now read off the task record on each request, through
ecs.metadata_task_status, and applied to the task route, the container route
and the Containers entries the task route carries.

Which member follows what is taken from a live task rather than guessed.
DesiredStatus is the task's everywhere: it flips to STOPPED while the task is
still RUNNING, and that is what a container polls to learn it is being shut
down. KnownStatus is the task's on the task payload and the container's own on
a container payload, because AWS reports them separately: a Fargate task
served "KnownStatus": "NONE" for the task and "KnownStatus": "RUNNING" for the
container in the same payload, read by that container while it was starting.

The task is looked up by the account and the region in its ARN. A container
reaches this endpoint with a path token and no SigV4, so the request resolves
under the default account and region, and keying the task store on those would
have missed every task created anywhere else.

The registered values are seeded from the record rather than from a literal,
so the only path that can serve them is a task whose record is gone, and there
the registered snapshot is the best answer available.

The two new tests live in tests/test_ecs_metadata.py, which already has the
registry fixture and the _call/_register helpers this needs.

The overlay is applied to a copy, because it writes the two members and the
dicts it is handed are the live registry entries: the task payload every
sibling container's /task view is built from, and the container payloads
inside it. Writing into those would drift the registry away from what was
registered, and the fallback for a task whose record is gone would then serve
a value nobody registered. json_response serialises immediately, so the
response itself was never a way to reach them; the copy is about the write,
not about the reader.

ecs_metadata imports ecs lazily inside the helper, because ecs imports
ecs_metadata; and the lookup runs outside the metadata lock, since the ecs
service takes its own per-task locks and holding both in that order would
invert them.

fix(cloudformation): provision AWS::IAM::Policy inline, as AWS does (#1716)

The document was stored as an account-global customer-managed policy and
attached to the Roles, Users and Groups the resource named. CloudFormation
embeds it on each of them instead, the way PutRolePolicy, PutUserPolicy and
PutGroupPolicy do.

An inline policy is scoped to its entity, so the same PolicyName can exist on
many entities at once. CDK relies on that: it derives PolicyName from the
construct path, so every stack granting something to a role reached by the same
path emits the same name. On one deployment twenty of twenty-seven policies
collapsed onto two records and each deploy took the grants away from the stacks
before it; under AUTH=true those roles were denied the actions their own
templates granted.

The document now goes onto each entity through the existing inline handlers, so
ListRolePolicies, GetRolePolicy, the RolePolicyList of
GetAccountAuthorizationDetails and the IAM evaluator all find it.

The physical id is generated rather than being the PolicyName, which is what
AWS answers: a stack with an explicit PolicyName of
ms0049-refprobe-explicit-name returns ms0049--Pol-AW24HieEB0iX from Ref. It is
returned unchanged on update, because the engine reads a changed physical id as
a replacement and the cleanup delete would remove the policy the update just
wrote.

AWS::IAM::ManagedPolicy is unchanged and keeps the four shared helpers. Two
helpers only AWS::IAM::Policy used are gone, along with iam.rename_policy,
which loses its only caller.

fix(iam): resolve the resource ARN so scoped policies match (#1719)

extract_resource_arn returned "*" for three whole families of request. A
resource-scoped policy can never match "*", so under AUTH=true the only grant
that worked was one written as Resource: "*". All three are false denials that
turn up the moment a CDK app is deployed.

IoT mapped six path prefixes to ARNs but not /jobs or /provisioning-templates,
and neither data plane had a branch at all. The CDK's AwsCustomResource for an
IoT job grants iot:CreateJob on exactly job/<jobId> plus the target
thinggroup/<name>, the scoping AWS documents, and a CloudFormation stack
carrying one fails here with "is not authorized to perform: iot:CreateJob"
while deploying on AWS.

The data planes are the same bug one level up. A client signs them with the
iotdata and iotjobsdata scopes, so detect_service answers iot-data and
iot-jobs-data, and a branch keyed on "iot" never runs. Both carry iot: actions
on iot: ARNs over the paths the map already names, so all three service keys
share one branch: a publish and a retained message resolve to their topic, a
shadow and a job execution to their thing. The topic carries every level. Its
ARN is topic/sensors/rack-1/temperature, so taking only the first segment after
/topics/ would authorize the publish against a different resource.

Publish had no action either, so it was not checked at all. Its URI label is
non-greedy, the SDK percent-encodes the separators to keep the value inside one
segment, and the ASGI server hands the path back decoded. A route compiled from
that label then matched no topic below the first level and extract_iam_action
returned None. iot-data's topic label is now compiled greedy, and the ARN is
unquoted so both spellings name one resource.

The query-protocol services put their parameters in a form-encoded body when
the SDK POSTs, which botocore does, so nothing reached the query string and
every branch that reads it resolved nothing. ec2:AuthorizeSecurityGroupIngress
scoped to one security group was denied for that security group. The router
already parses that body to find Action and threw the rest away; it now keeps
it, merged underneath the query string, which still wins. Keeping the merge
there also keeps it gated on the one content type that can carry it, and off
the S3 upload path, where extract_resource_arn runs over bodies that are large.

An execute-api invoke was authorized against "*" too, so a policy naming one
API and stage never matched. It now resolves to
arn:aws:execute-api:<region>:<account>:<api-id>/<stage>/<METHOD>/<path>, built
by the same helper the Lambda authorizer's method ARN uses, because a policy
has to match both and there were already two copies of that string. The stage
is resolved before the check rather than after: a v2 API on $default serves
from the root, so the first path segment is not a stage there, and naming it
one would authorize against a resource that does not exist. That resolution
only reads the API's configured stages, and it answers a caller who is not
authorized yet, so it reports nothing about why it failed.

None of the three can introduce a false allow: a request that resolved to "*"
before now resolves to its own ARN, so a Resource: "*" grant still matches and
a scoped grant starts matching only what it names.

The redundant cert branch, whose two arms built the same string, goes with it.

fix(iam): authorize a Secrets Manager request against the stored secret ARN (#1737)

Under AUTH=true a Secrets Manager request was evaluated against
secret:<name>, built from the SecretId. AWS evaluates against the stored
ARN, which carries the six random characters minted at CreateSecret. The
grant the CDK writes for a secret looked up by name is
secret:<name>-?????? or secret:<name>-*, so it matched nothing here.

GetSecretValue on secret:<name>-0ac6da and denies secret:<name>.

extract_resource_arn now reads the stored ARN through
secretsmanager._resolve, the lookup the request handlers use. A short
name, a full ARN and an ARN without the suffix resolve alike, scoped to
the request's account and region. An unknown secret keeps the
name-derived ARN.

secret:<name> without a wildcard denies, as on AWS. AUTH off is
unchanged.

fix(iam): validate a group policy document and fail on a missing entity (#1738)

PutGroupPolicy stored any document, while PutRolePolicy and
PutUserPolicy refused a malformed one. The group handler validates now.
All three resolve the entity first: measured on AWS, a missing group,
role or user with a malformed document answers NoSuchEntity.
PutRolePolicy uses the measured sentence "The role with name <name>
cannot be found.".

An AWS::IAM::Policy naming a Role, User or Group that does not exist was
skipped, so the stack reported CREATE_COMPLETE. AWS fails the resource

A template declaring AWS::LanguageExtensions was provisioned as sent. An
Fn::ForEach key reached the engine as a resource with a list definition,
the deploy task died on an AttributeError and the stack stayed in
CREATE_IN_PROGRESS. Fn::ToJsonString was stored as a dict.

The transform now runs over Resources, Conditions and Outputs after
AWS::Include and before SAM. Fn::ForEach iterates a literal array, a Ref
to a CommaDelimitedList parameter, Fn::FindInMap or Fn::Split, nests, and
may sit inside Properties. Measured substitution rule: the identifier is
replaced in a fragment key, in ${Id} inside Fn::Sub and through a Ref to
the identifier; a plain string value, &{Id} inside Fn::Sub and nested
keys keep the placeholder. Fn::Length and Fn::ToJsonString (compact JSON)
are resolved; a ToJsonString member only the stack knows (Fn::GetAtt, a
pseudo parameter) is resolved by the engine. The Fn::FindInMap lookup is
shared with the engine.

Refused before a stack exists, with the measured sentence where there is
one: a malformed loop, a non-array collection, Fn::Select out of range,
Fn::Length over a stack value, a Condition naming no condition, a logical
id or output key that becomes non-alphanumeric, a nested Fn::Sub variable
name (${Param${Item}}), and a transform function in a template that does
not declare the transform. ValidateTemplate refuses the undeclared loop
as well. Neither ValidateTemplate nor GetTemplateSummary expands the
template; the summary then omits ResourceTypes and Capabilities, as on
AWS.

The expansion counts against the template quotas. UsePreviousTemplate
reuses the processed template and does not re-expand for a new parameter
value, as measured.

fix(apigateway): gateway responses, AWS error answers and MOCK status selection (#1756)

* fix(apigateway): apply gateway responses to gateway errors

PutGatewayResponse stored a customization that nothing on the data plane read.
Every error API Gateway emits itself was a fixed status and a fixed body, so a
CDK stack adding CORS headers to its 401s and 403s, the common reason to
declare one, got no headers in the browser.

Each gateway error now carries its response type and is answered through the
response in effect: the customized entry for the type, else a customized
DEFAULT_4XX or DEFAULT_5XX by the type's default status family, else the
built-in default. A specific entry replaces the family entry. Header mappings
resolve quoted literals, request headers (case-insensitive), path and query
parameters, stage variables and context.requestId, and a missing source omits
the header. The application/json template renders $context.error.message,
messageString and responseType, $context.requestId, resourcePath and stage,
whatever the request accepts. The error carries x-amzn-ErrorType, and the
x-amzn-RequestId header is the id the body rendered.

The responses in effect are the ones CreateDeployment captured for the stage's
deployment, as on AWS: a Put or Delete without a redeploy leaves the data
plane unchanged. AWS::ApiGateway::GatewayResponse goes through the same path
and needs nothing of its own.

On the control plane a response put without templates stores the default
application/json template, and an uncustomized type reports the templates and
parameters of the DEFAULT_4XX or DEFAULT_5XX it inherits, with its own status
code and defaultResponse true.

Status codes and messages at each error site are unchanged here.

* fix(apigateway): answer gateway errors with the AWS status and message

With the gateway responses in place, the error sites still reported what the
emulator used to invent. Measured against AWS:

An explicit Deny from a Lambda authorizer says "User is not authorized to
access this resource with an explicit deny in an identity-based policy".

An authorizer that raises is AUTHORIZER_FAILURE with a null message, so the
default body is {"message":null}.

An AWS_PROXY integration naming a missing function and an HTTP_PROXY backend
that does not resolve or times out are API_CONFIGURATION_ERROR: 500 and
"Internal server error" instead of 502 and the exception text. AWS renders
that type's $context.error.messageString with a leading space, and the default
body keeps it.

An authorizer naming a missing function is AUTHORIZER_CONFIGURATION_ERROR:
the customized entry, its status code and x-amzn-ErrorType
AuthorizerConfigurationException apply, while the template variables render
as for API_CONFIGURATION_ERROR ($context.error.responseType is
API_CONFIGURATION_ERROR, messageString with the leading space). $context.status
renders empty in a gateway response.

An unknown stage is 403 {"message":"Forbidden"} with ForbiddenException, and
no gateway response applies to it.

An authorizer that returns a policy without principalId is not a
configuration error: AWS evaluates the policy and the Allow reaches the
integration, for a TOKEN and for a REQUEST authorizer alike.

* fix(apigateway): select MOCK integration responses by template statusCode

A MOCK integration always answered through its "200" integration response,
whatever statusCode the request template set. That is how a MOCK method models
an error, so a request template of {"statusCode": 500} with an integration
response whose selectionPattern is "500" returned 200 and the success body.

The statusCode in the application/json request template is now the
integration status, 200 when absent. The response whose selectionPattern
matches it is selected; when several match, the entry whose own status code
is the integration status wins, so a catch-all pattern on another entry does
not shadow the exact one. The previous order applies when none matches. AWS
answers that case with 500 and the mapped body, without x-amzn-ErrorType.

feat(cloudformation): twelve update handlers, ECR through the store, replaced resources kept until success (#1757)

* feat(cloudformation): update handlers for twelve more types (ELBv2, Route53, WAFv2, Backup, ACM, SES, IoT, API Gateway)

Without an update handler a stack update re-runs the create. Measured on
main: the four ELBv2 types took new ARNs and lost registered targets,
AWS::Route53::HostedZone took a new zone id and orphaned its record sets,
AWS::WAFv2::WebACL and AWS::Backup::BackupPlan took new ids, an ACM
certificate was re-issued on a tag change, AWS::SES::EmailIdentity lost
its DKIM tokens, AWS::Backup::BackupVault never saw a tag change,
AWS::ApiGateway::Account kept a dropped role, and AWS::IoT::ThingType
failed with ResourceAlreadyExistsException.

Each type now updates in place for the properties its reference marks
"No interruption" and replaces for "Replacement", through the shared
rename path, so UpdateReplacePolicy Retain keeps the predecessor. The
load balancer, target group, web ACL and thing type join the custom-name
refusal table; the backup vault refuses an EncryptionKeyArn change the
same way, because its name is required.

Thing type, measured on AWS: Mqtt5Configuration updates in place and is
cleared when the template drops it. A ThingTypeDescription or
SearchableAttributes change under a custom name fails with the
custom-named-resource sentence. Under a generated name the type is
re-created; the name is deterministic, so Retain cannot keep it.

Four defects the tests depend on are fixed as well: a stack's backup plan
read back without rules, its email identity was missing from the SES v2
store, DescribeTags raised on its target groups (tags stored as a map),
and ACM timestamps answered the time of the call.

Twenty-one tests with twenty-six cases; twenty fail on main, the other
six guard replacement paths the fall-through already produced.

Part of #1601 (item C1, the types without an update handler are
re-created on a property change).

* fix(cloudformation): provision ECR repositories through the ECR store

AWS::ECR::Repository built its record by hand. Scanning and encryption
settings were stored in PascalCase and read back empty, LifecyclePolicy,
RepositoryPolicyText and Tags were dropped, PutImage into the repository
failed with InternalError, and the delete popped only the repository
record (read from the source). Measured on AWS, the same template reads back every property
and updates mutability, scanning, lifecycle policy and tags in place.

Create, update and delete now go through the ECR service functions
(CreateRepository, PutLifecyclePolicy, SetRepositoryPolicy,
DeleteRepository) with one translation helper. The type joins the
stack-tag table. A repository that still holds images fails the delete
unless EmptyOnDelete is true, as the API does (measured: the stack ends
DELETE_FAILED and the repository survives). A RepositoryName change is a
replacement: the new repository is created and the old one deleted through
the predecessor path, so UpdateReplacePolicy retains it.

Not covered: refusing a duplicate repository name on create (AWS fails the
stack at validation, measured), and the change-set Replacement
classification.

* fix(cloudformation): keep the replaced resource until the update succeeds

An update handler that replaces its resource deleted the predecessor as
soon as the replacement existed. When a later resource failed, the
rollback deleted the replacement as well, and the stack landed in
UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE recording physical ids that no longer existed.
Measured with a renamed SSM parameter and SQS queue: old and new were gone
for both. On AWS (measured for the SSM parameter) the new parameter is deleted
during rollback cleanup and the old one survives; after a successful
update the predecessor is deleted in the cleanup phase (documented).

_delete_predecessor now queues the delete when the stack engine collects
them, and the engine runs the queue in its replacement cleanup, which only
runs once the update succeeded. The cleanup walks the replacements in
reverse order, so a dependent goes before what it depends on, and reads
UpdateReplacePolicy as before. Output resolution moves ahead of both
cleanups, so an output that fails the update no longer leaves predecessors
or removed resources deleted. A replacement under an unchanged physical id
(subscription filter, resource server, API Gateway model) is undone on
rollback by its new properties.

Nested stack children keep deleting at once: the child has no cleanup
phase of its own.

Not covered, the old resource is still lost on rollback:
- DynamoDB table, Location tracker and IoT thing type under a generated
  name, which delete and recreate under the same deterministic name
- an EventBridge rule moved to another bus, whose handler moves the record
- resources inside a nested stack

fix(iot): registered-certificate event on connect, retired endpoint types, $ topics (#1755)

* fix(iot): publish the registered-certificate event on the first mTLS connect

RegisterCertificate published $aws/events/certificates/registered/{caId}
when the CA was ACTIVE with auto-registration enabled. On AWS the call
publishes nothing (measured for INACTIVE and ACTIVE, 45 to 60 s), and
status PENDING_ACTIVATION is refused with CertificateStateException 406,
by RegisterCertificateWithoutCA as well (measured).

AWS publishes the event on an mTLS connect instead. A certificate that is
unknown, signed by an ACTIVE CA with autoRegistrationStatus ENABLE, is
created PENDING_ACTIVATION with caCertificateId, the event carries
certificateRegistrationTimestamp null and sourceIp, and the server closes
without a CONNACK. A repeat connect while PENDING_ACTIVATION publishes
again with the creation time in epoch milliseconds as a string. An
INACTIVE certificate gets no event; a CA with auto-registration
disabled gets no event and no certificate is created.

The listener now does this before its CONNACK 5 refusal, which stays for
every other case. The record shape and the guarded publish move into
shared helpers, so the register APIs and the listener build the same
record.

* fix(iot): refuse DescribeEndpoint for the retired iot:Data and iot:Jobs types

Both endpoint types returned a hostname. AWS answers 400
InvalidRequestException for both, with "iot:Data is not supported.
Please use iot:Data-ATS instead." and, for iot:Jobs, a message pointing
the jobs APIs at iot:Data-ATS. The emulator now returns the same errors.

The jobs routing test took its Host from DescribeEndpoint(iot:Jobs); it
now sets the host directly, since the router still accepts that shape.

* fix(iot-data): refuse a publish to a topic that starts with $

HTTPS Publish accepted every topic, so a caller could publish a forged
$aws/events/... message and fire the topic rules on it, and the MQTT
broker acknowledged the same publish with a PUBACK.

Measured over 42 HTTPS publishes: AWS refuses a topic starting with $
with 400 InvalidRequestException "Topic can't start with $", except under
$aws/rules/, $aws/things/, $aws/certificates/, $aws/provisioning-templates/
and $aws/device_location/. The bare $aws/rules, $aws/things and
$aws/certificates are refused too. Jobs topics ($aws/things/<t>/jobs/...),
defender/metrics/json and one $aws/commands/ topic answer 400 "Invalid
publish to restricted topic using HTTP"; the emulator applies that answer
to the whole defender/ and commands/ prefixes, measured on one topic each.
Shadow, basic ingest and tunnel topics publish as before.

Over MQTT 3.1.1 (measured with an ACTIVE certificate holding an allow-all
policy) AWS acknowledges a publish under $aws/rules/ and $aws/things/ and
closes the connection without a PUBACK for $aws/events/..., $aws/jobs/...
and $foo/.... The broker now closes the connection for a $ topic outside
the same prefix list; an MQTT 5 client gets a DISCONNECT with reason
0x87, which is not measured. The prefix list lives in iot.py and the
HTTPS handler reads it from there.

The emulator's own shadow and jobs publishes go through the broker's
internal path, not this check. The jobs MQTT bridge tests drove the bridge
through HTTPS Publish; they now publish over MQTT.

Record direct-to-phone SNS publishes and serve them back (#1682)

* feat(sns): record direct-to-phone publishes and serve them back

A Publish carrying a PhoneNumber and no TopicArn logged one line and stored
nothing, so an SMS was the only thing a suite could send through MiniStack and
not observe. SES and SQS both keep what they were sent and serve it at
/_ministack/ses/messages and /_ministack/sqs/messages; SNS now does the same.

Publishes are kept per account and per region and served at
GET /_ministack/sns/sms-messages, grouped by recipient and filterable by
phoneNumber, account and region. The same body is served at LocalStack's
GET /_aws/sns/sms-messages in LocalStack's
{"sms_messages": {"<phone>": [...]}, "region": "<region>"} shape, the same
compatibility /_localstack/health already has, so a suite that asserts an SMS
was sent runs here unedited. A filtered read names the recipient with an empty
list rather than omitting the key, as LocalStack does.

The log is cleared by /_ministack/reset and rides the existing sns persistence
entry. Topic publishes are unaffected and are not recorded.

* fix(sns): drop the /_aws/ alias, keep the native SMS-log path

Review asked for this, and the reasoning holds: MiniStack keeps the
compatibility surface narrow. `/_ministack/ses/messages` and
`/_ministack/sqs/messages` carry no `/_aws/` alias either, and one is worth
adding only against a concrete migration it would otherwise make painful.
None was named, so the alias goes.

What made it easy to agree: the compatibility that actually matters is in
the BODY, not the URL. The response keeps LocalStack's
`{"sms_messages": {"<phone>": [...]}, "region": "<region>"}` shape, so a
suite moving here changes one string and nothing else — and that is
unchanged by this commit.

The alias test is adapted rather than deleted: it asserted the two paths
returned identical bodies, and now asserts the native path serves the same
body while `/_aws/sns/sms-messages` answers 404. The invariant it guards is
inverted, not dropped, so a future change that quietly re-adds the alias
still fails a test.

README and CHANGELOG both advertised the alias; both now name only the
native path.

feat(cloudformation): update 16 more types in place, roll back in-place changes, ECS cluster settings and EC2 stack tags (#1796)

* feat(cloudformation): update AppConfig applications, environments, configuration profiles and deployment strategies in place

None of the four AppConfig types had an update handler. A change to any
property re-ran the create, and the resource came back under a new
generated id. Its children were orphaned: environments and configuration
profiles are keyed by the application id, hosted configuration versions
by the application and profile id.

Each type now updates in place the properties its resource reference
lists as No interruption, and replaces on the others. The replacement
goes through _rename_replacement, so UpdateReplacePolicy: Retain and the
deferred delete of the predecessor work as for the other types.

- Application: Description, Name and Tags are No interruption. The type
  has no property that requires a replacement.
- Environment: ApplicationId is Replacement. DeletionProtectionCheck,
  Description, Monitors, Name and Tags are No interruption.
- ConfigurationProfile: ApplicationId, LocationUri and Type are
  Replacement and are compared as one key. The other properties update
  in place.
- DeploymentStrategy: Name and ReplicateTo are Replacement. Ref answers
  the generated strategy id, so a rename is a plain replacement with no
  custom name to refuse.

AppConfig keeps tags in a map per ARN beside the record. One helper runs
the shared tag reconcile against that map, so tags set through
TagResource stay.

Measured on AWS: a configuration profile update keeps the profile id and
its hosted configuration version, also on a second update, and the stack
delete removes the application.

Part of #1601 (item C1).

* feat(cloudformation): update AppSync GraphQL APIs and API keys in place

AWS::AppSync::GraphQLApi and AWS::AppSync::ApiKey had no update handler,
so a property change re-ran the create.

For the API, the create minted a new api id and seeded empty stores for
its keys, data sources, resolvers and types. A renamed API came back
empty, and the old one stayed behind with every child the stack had
created. The resource reference lists every GraphQLApi property as No
interruption. The handler keeps the id, the ARN and the endpoint URLs
and applies the change in place.

The API record now holds what the template sets, in AppSync's camelCase,
on create and on update: AdditionalAuthenticationProviders, XrayEnabled,
QueryDepthLimit, ResolverCountLimit, IntrospectionConfig,
EnvironmentVariables, OwnerContact, LogConfig, UserPoolConfig,
OpenIDConnectConfig, LambdaAuthorizerConfig, EnhancedMetricsConfig and
MergedApiExecutionRoleArn. AdditionalAuthenticationProviders was kept in
the template's PascalCase, so GetGraphqlApi answered [{}]. The others
were not stored at all. A member the template removes goes back to
AppSync's default or is dropped. OpenIDConnectConfig answers both TTLs,
0 when unset. ApiType is set at create only, because UpdateGraphqlApi
has no member for it.

A Visibility change fails the update with AWS's message: "Property
Visibility can only be set when creating a GraphQL API. Rename the
resource to force a replacement". AWS wraps it in "Resource handler
returned message: ...". The emulator gives the inner text only.

The API carries the template's tags and the stack-level tags. AppSync
does not list the aws:cloudformation: tags on the API, so they are left
out.

The api id now has the 26 characters that CreateGraphqlApi mints. With
eight, the ARN was too short and botocore refused it for
ListTagsForResource. The API also answers the REALTIME endpoint beside
GRAPHQL, as CreateGraphqlApi does.

The create of an API key mints a new key id. Under the fallback every
Expires change handed out a new key and left the previous one valid on
the API. The resource reference lists Description and Expires as No
interruption and ApiId as Replacement. The key record also carries
description and createdAt now, which CreateApiKey writes. Before,

* fix(cloudformation): roll back in-place updates

An update rollback kept every resource that existed before the update,
with its physical id, but did not undo what the update had changed on
it. The stack recorded the old template while the resource kept the new
properties. 1.5.8 shipped this as a known limitation ("An in-place
change is not reverted"), and a test pinned it: VisibilityTimeout read
45 after the rollback.

AWS rolls an update back as an update to the previous template. The
changes made in place go back first, then what the update created is
deleted in a cleanup phase.

The rollback now does the same. Each resource that kept its identity and
was changed goes back through its type's update handler, from the
properties the update applied to the previous ones. Stack tags are added
on both sides as the forward update did. The revert records
UPDATE_IN_PROGRESS and UPDATE_COMPLETE events. An unchanged resource is
not called. The emulator reverts one resource after the other in the
template's dependency order. AWS reverts them in parallel.

The resource whose update failed comes last. A custom resource or a
nested stack is sent back too, because its provider may have changed
state before it failed. For any other type the handler refused the
update and changed nothing, so it only gets an UPDATE_COMPLETE event and
is not called again.

The events follow AWS. UPDATE_ROLLBACK_IN_PROGRESS names the failed
resource: "The following resource(s) failed to update: [X]. ", or
"failed to create" for a resource the update added. It said "Rollback
requested". The stack then goes to
UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE_CLEANUP_IN_PROGRESS, and each resource the
update created is deleted with DELETE_IN_PROGRESS and DELETE_COMPLETE
events. The final UPDATE_ROLLBACK_COMPLETE has no reason.

A delete that fails in the cleanup phase is a DELETE_FAILED event and
nothing more. The rollback is complete by then, so it no longer turns
the stack into UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED. A revert that fails does: the
stack lands in UPDATE_ROLLBACK_FAILED with "The following resource(s)
failed to update: [...]". ContinueUpdateRollback retries such a revert,
or skips it, as it does with a failed delete.

An executed change set that rolls back also restores the stack's
parameters. The execute path did not keep them, so DescribeStacks
reported the values of the update that had just been undone.

Measured on AWS: an SQS queue whose VisibilityTimeout went from 30 to 45
reads 30 after the rollback, and the queue the update added is deleted
in the cleanup phase. In-place changes on a VPC, a subnet, a security
group, an Auto Scaling group, a scaling policy, a scheduled action, an
AppSync API and an AppConfig application, failed by a later resource,
read their old values after the rollback. A custom resource whose update
answered FAILED is sent its update back. A scaling policy refused with
AlreadyExists gets a single UPDATE_COMPLETE event. A rolled back change
set restores the parameter.

S3: event notification records match S3's (#1832)

The object block of a notification record now carries what S3 documents
(S3 User Guide, "Event message structure"):

- versionId: the version a create made, or the version or delete marker a

record can name it.

* S3: object annotations

Adds PutObjectAnnotation, GetObjectAnnotation, ListObjectAnnotations and
DeleteObjectAnnotation, and annotations' part in CopyObject, versioning,
deletes, replication, encryption, Object Lock, persistence and event
notifications. Before this a PUT ?annotation fell through to PutObject and
replaced the object with the annotation's payload.

The four operations (S3 API Reference, botocore model 1.43.63):
- Put: a named UTF-8 payload of 1 byte to 1 MiB, up to 1,000 per object
  version; the naming rules of "Annotation naming rules"
  (InvalidAnnotationName, AnnotationNameTooLong), AnnotationLimitExceeded,
  UnsupportedMediaType, and x-amz-object-if-match against the object's ETag
- Get: NoSuchAnnotation for a name the version does not have; stored
  checksums only with x-amz-checksum-mode: ENABLED
- List: UTF-8 name order, annotation-prefix, max-annotation-results (1 to
  1000) and continuation tokens, with each entry's size, ETag, checksum
  algorithms, last-modified time and replication status
- Delete: 204, also for a name that is not there; Object Lock governance
  retention needs x-amz-bypass-governance-retention

From "Annotating your objects":
- An annotation belongs to one object version. A new version starts with
  none; deleting a version deletes its annotations; a delete marker leaves
  the version's alone; an unversioned or suspended overwrite, or a delete,
  drops them. Writing one changes neither the object's ETag nor its version.
- CopyObject copies them unless x-amz-object-annotation-directive is EXCLUDE,
  and a copy that names a checksum algorithm recomputes theirs with it.
- A payload's checksum is verified when sent (BadDigest) and defaults to
  CRC64NVME. CRC32, CRC32C, CRC64NVME, SHA1, SHA256, SHA512, MD5 and XXHASH64
  are computed (XXH64 in the stdlib, checked against the reference values);
  XXHASH3 and XXHASH128 are refused, as PutObject refuses algorithms it
  cannot verify, rather than stored unchecked.
- Annotations take the object's encryption (SSE-S3 when it has none) and are
  refused on SSE-C objects; they replicate with the object (COMPLETED on the
  source, REPLICA on the replica).

Events ("Event notification types and destinations", "Event message
structure"): s3:ObjectAnnotation:Put and s3:ObjectAnnotation:Delete, with the
record's objectAnnotation block (name, and size and eTag on Put) and no
object-level event; Get and List send none; a CopyObject event reports
hasObjectAnnotation.

Annotations persist per version with S3_PERSIST=1, in the key's sidecar
beside tags and ACLs, and reset() clears them.

Not included: the S3 Metadata annotation table
(UpdateBucketMetadataAnnotationTableConfiguration), since MiniStack has no
S3 Metadata configuration for it to belong to, and event notifications for
annotations replicated to another bucket.

Where the documentation is silent the code says so: the ordering of List,
the refusal of a versionId naming a delete marker (as a read of one), and
Object Lock compliance mode and legal holds refusing a delete as they refuse
the object's own.

Evidence: official AWS documentation and the botocore service model. Not
validated against a real AWS account. tests/test_s3_annotations.py (48 tests)
covers each behaviour; 40 of them fail on 1.5.17.

fix(lambda): report a bare-string RIE timeout as a function error (#1855)

The RIE can end a run that hit the function timeout with HTTP 200 and the
plain body "Task timed out after N.00 seconds". It is not JSON, so it
was returned as a successful payload and Step Functions recorded
TaskSucceeded without running Catch.

Classify that exact text as Unhandled and give it the same
{errorMessage, errorType: Runtime.ExitError} body as the read-timeout
path. Fixes #1845.

fix(cloudformation): delete the resources a nested stack's update drops (#1858)

The nested stack deploy starts the child's resource map from the
previous resources and writes the updated ones into that same dict,
so the removal set set(prev_resources) - set(provisioned) was always
empty. A resource removed from the child template stayed in its
service and in DescribeStackResources of the child. The same applied
to a failed child update that the parent rolled back: the resource
the failed update had created was never deleted.

CloudFormation updates the resources of a modified nested stack when
the parent is updated, and a resource that leaves a template is
removed ("Remove (deletes a resource)" in the ResourceChange API
reference); a failed update rolls back and deletes what it created.

The removal set is now computed against the resources the new child
template declares, as for a top-level stack, and a deleted resource
leaves the child's resource map. The map keeps starting from the
previous resources, so a child update that fails half way still knows
every resource the rollback has to restore.

fix(cloudformation): apply every AWS::SQS::Queue property (#1859)

The AWS::SQS::Queue provisioner copied five numeric properties and
ContentBasedDeduplication into the queue and dropped the rest:
RedrivePolicy, RedriveAllowPolicy, KmsMasterKeyId,
KmsDataKeyReusePeriodSeconds, SqsManagedSseEnabled, DeduplicationScope
and FifoThroughputLimit. The stack reached CREATE_COMPLETE, but
GetQueueAttributes showed none of them, so a dead-letter queue declared
in a template never received a message. The provisioner also skipped the
checks CreateQueue and SetQueueAttributes run, so a queue with
MessageRetentionPeriod 10 was created.

The resource reference lists all of these properties with Update
requires: No interruption; RedrivePolicy and RedriveAllowPolicy are Json
there and strings in the SQS API. On AWS a MessageRetentionPeriod of 10
fails the queue with CREATE_FAILED and "Invalid value for the parameter
MessageRetentionPeriod." from SQS, and the stack rolls back.

Create and update now build the attribute map in one helper, which
renders Json properties as compact JSON strings, as GetQueueAttributes
returns them on AWS, and booleans as true/false, and validates the map
with the SQS module's own RedrivePolicy and numeric range checks. A
refused value fails the resource with the SQS message. On update a
property the template drops is removed from the queue; the queue URL and
its messages stay.

fix(cloudformation): send change set members as AWS does for each action (#1860)

DescribeChangeSet put Replacement False on Add and Remove changes, sent
no PhysicalResourceId on Remove and Modify, never sent PolicyAction, and
left RequiresRecreation out of Metadata, DeletionPolicy and
UpdateReplacePolicy details.

Change sets created in eu-central-1 show what AWS sends: no Replacement
on Add or Remove, the physical id on Remove and Modify, PolicyAction
Delete on a Remove and ReplaceAndDelete on every Modify with Replacement
True, no PolicyAction on an in-place or conditional Modify, and
RequiresRecreation Never on attribute details.

_diff_resources now takes the stack's resources for the physical id,
drops Replacement from Add and Remove, and sets PolicyAction when the
applicable DeletionPolicy or UpdateReplacePolicy is Delete. A Retain or
Snapshot policy leaves PolicyAction out, as its AWS value has not been
observed. Attribute details report RequiresRecreation Never, and
DescribeChangeSet writes PolicyAction when a change has one.

fix(iam): a negated operator applies to an absent key, and BatchGetSecretValue checks each secret (#1861)

* fix(iam): an absent condition key makes a negated operator true

_evaluate_single_condition returned False for any operator whose key is
absent from the request context, unless the operator was an IfExists
or ForAllValues form. For a negated operator AWS does the opposite: a
Deny conditioned on StringNotEquals aws:PrincipalTag/team = blue denies
a request that carries no such tag. Under AUTH=true that Deny never
applied here.

Measured per operator with iam simulate-custom-policy. With the key
absent, StringNotEquals, StringNotEqualsIgnoreCase, StringNotLike,
NumericNotEquals, DateNotEquals, ArnNotEquals, ArnNotLike and
NotIpAddress evaluate to true. ForAnyValue stays false for negated
operators too, ForAllValues and IfExists stay true, and every
affirmative operator stays false.

This can turn a request that was allowed into a denied one for
policies that rely on the old behaviour; it now matches AWS.

* fix(secretsmanager): check GetSecretValue per secret in BatchGetSecretValue

Under AUTH=true BatchGetSecretValue was authorized once, as
secretsmanager:BatchGetSecretValue on *, and then returned every
secret it named. A caller without secretsmanager:GetSecretValue on a
secret could read it this way. Filters were ignored as well, so a
filtered call returned every secret in the store.

Measured on AWS with a user holding BatchGetSecretValue on * and
GetSecretValue on one of two secrets: the call succeeds, returns the
readable secret and reports the other in Errors as
AccessDeniedException, naming the resource as the request named it. A
call by Filters is refused as a whole without
secretsmanager:ListSecrets and, with it, applies the same per-secret
check to the matching secrets, reported by ARN. A missing secret stays
ResourceNotFoundException.

The handler now evaluates GetSecretValue against each secret's stored
ARN, checks ListSecrets when the request selects by Filters, and
selects those secrets with the filter logic ListSecrets already uses,
now shared. Without AUTH only the Filters selection changes.

fix(cloudformation): honor OnFailure, DeletionMode, TemplateStage and ClientRequestToken (#1877)

* fix(cloudformation): honor OnFailure, DeletionMode, TemplateStage and ClientRequestToken

- CreateStack OnFailure: DO_NOTHING keeps a failed create in CREATE_FAILED,
  DELETE rolls back and then deletes the stack; OnFailure together with
  DisableRollback is a ValidationError.
- CreateChangeSet OnStackFailure applies the same choice on execute; DELETE
  is refused unless ChangeSetType is CREATE, DescribeChangeSet reports it,
  and ExecuteChangeSet refuses DisableRollback for such a change set.
  ExecuteChangeSet DisableRollback=true is honored (it was ignored).
- DeleteStack DeletionMode=FORCE_DELETE_STACK on a DELETE_FAILED stack
  retains the resources that failed to delete and their dependencies
  (DELETE_SKIPPED) and reaches DELETE_COMPLETE; other statuses are refused.
- GetTemplate TemplateStage=Processed returns the template after its
  transforms, StagesAvailable lists both stages, and ChangeSetName returns
  a change set's template. Original stays the default.
- Stack events carry the ClientRequestToken of the operation that recorded
  them; an invalid token is a ValidationError.

fix(iot): check the verification certificate in RegisterCACertificate (#1881)

In DEFAULT mode RegisterCACertificate registered any CA, with or without a
verificationCertificate, and nothing consumed the code GetRegistrationCode
returns. The call now requires a verification certificate that the CA
signed and whose CN is the registration code, refuses one in SNI_ONLY mode,
and answers each failure with the error code and message AWS returns. The
checks run before the duplicate check, as on AWS. AWS::IoT::CACertificate
goes through the same path, so a DEFAULT-mode resource without
VerificationCertificatePem now fails.

Tests that register a CA get the verification certificate from one shared
helper, iot_test_ca in tests/conftest.py.

fix(rds): keep database containers reachable under MINISTACK_RDS_PUBLIC_ENDPOINT (#1885)

With the setting on, database containers were left off MiniStack's network
and readiness dialled 127.0.0.1:<host port>. Inside a containerised
MiniStack that address is MiniStack's own container, so instances and
clusters stayed `creating` forever. A containerised MiniStack now keeps its
database containers on its network for readiness and internal wiring, and
still reports {MINISTACK_HOST, host_port} for instance, writer and reader
endpoints; a host-run MiniStack is unchanged.

Fixes #1884.
